paragraphs.text: THE POEMS OF MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS.
BOOK ONE.
1. JOURNEY TO THE FORT OF BRIGANTIO.
Titan had climbed higher up the star-bearing axis,
when with his full lamp he shows himself to the whole world.
The flame-bearer was drinking up the rivers in the burning Crab,
when the reaper masters his own harvest with the sickle.
While a man is parched even as he drinks from the spring, while the world pants,
I was ordered out on a journey into the wilds of Gaul,
and I did not fear the scorching fields that outdo Syene.
Dust, flame and thirst were the dowry of my obedience.
Why, Muse, do you renew for me the blazing sun and the fierce heat?
It will be a greater thing to have conquered the freezing roads.
Whatever burns on the plains, whatever stiffens with cold on the heights,
say that I endured it all beneath a lawless sky.
The war of nature that the discordant year had waged,
a single day brought both summer and winter.
Wrapped in clouds, the poet, still hot, was taught by command
to master the white frosts.
A cloak of summer weight had covered my body;
clothed in a thin covering, I was as good as naked.
while time fled from my eyes though the season stayed constant [?],
for the lamp of Phoebus was my guide to the ice.
I had wished for winter, and from my wish came shivering,
and the warmth I sought gave no sign of itself.
I say nothing of the crags and trackless places called the Matrons,
alluring at the entrance, harsh in all the rest.
Their painted face enticed wretched travellers;
once trodden, they soon gave birth to dreadful deaths.
Hallowed antiquity is not at all misleading in its proper names,
choosing to call so many forms of death by this name.
The rugged path hung where footholds broke away,
and, believe me, the track was not easy even to look at.
Why, fame of the ancients, do you wrap up in your tongues the recesses of the labyrinth,
which one retracing them would fear?
There the craftsman's maze stood worthy of praise,
when Daedalus twisted the straight path by his ingenuity.
Here nature carries men across the summit of Olympus,
where only a dove can go, gliding through the liquid air.
Spare me, Pierides, and keep silent about the sea of rivers,
lest speech revive what good fortune [?] has driven away.
For the Duria, the torrent Sessis, the Stura or the Orgus
outdo the savagery of the Ionian sea.
When sweet joys follow various dangers,
the happy outcome tends to steady the heart.
I want nothing more to do with perils; forgetfulness helps the sad:
I carry a heart drunk from the spring of Lethe.
Better to have visited, trembling, the thresholds of the saints,
and to have shown my tears to the martyrs.
See, Saturninus, Crispinus, Daria, Maurus,
Eusebius and Quintus prepare great joys.
Octavius, grant it to my deserts; Adventor, restore; Solutor,
let not a white life fall into dark stains.
Let a mind conscious of right tear apart the snares of the enemy:
may this always please me: what is fitting, may that be permitted.
2. A SPEECH COMPOSED FOR DEUTERIUS, V.S., GRAMMARIAN, TO BE SENT IN HIS OWN NAME TO EUGENETES, V.I.
Joys surpass one's powers; the glad voice exults:
good fortune does not fear a meagre wit.
Sweet strings serve in favourable times:
what the fortunate man has deserved will become a noble song.
The quaestor, voice of the just, substance of the laws,
will send us, like Phoebus, drums, plectrum and lyre.
Let the learned and devoted band of the sister Camenae gather,
and offer with nimble thumb what it speaks.
The swelling breast of a prophetic bard could scarcely
count up the kinds of your virtues.
You glory of Italy, you most faithful hope of right,
torch and trumpet of causes, our purple, hail!
Lofty Rome, rich in luminaries, has called you the sun,
receiving you into her Quirinal bosom.
With your eloquence you subdue the lynx, with your voice the lion.
By your honey the serpent holds back the weapons of its throat.
Tigresses robbed of their young would bring you gifts,
such as grief and fierceness would give [?].
When the hand of fate was tearing at you, all but cut down like a flower,
Christ struck down destruction.
The blessed man's life, restored, now surpasses itself;
his deeds declare that it came from above.
Relying on these things, I have not drawn out envoys or the cunning words
of petitioners by painted arts.
I myself, sending you the words of a beggarly Thalia,
pray that you grant a gift, as God does.
A little garden, joined to a tiny plot, holds back
my hope from being complete, so that I cannot become its owner.
Do not scorn to bestow it on me, light of honours:
so may you, your wishes fulfilled, adorn our age,
so may the lofty power of the ruler raise you high,
so may golden deeds keep pace with your merits.
Whatever Dircean Amphion touched with his plectrum came alive:
nothing, once given life, could then die.
No benefits have flowed to me from the Muses in so many years;
win them for me by the warmth of your bounty.
3. PREFACE SPOKEN FOR THE GRANDSONS OF PROCULUS ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY.
Now the fruitful earth presses out her teats into the ear of grain,
swelling with milk in the wedded turf.
The sap spread through the grasses is drawn together into offspring,
making from drops a solid progeny.
The vine-shoot, clothed with buds, stretches out its arms;
see, from the bosom of the wood the vine-leaf grows green.
The vine, bidden now to lose its leafy wood for the sake of growth,
is won over by its wounds, so that it may grow in fruit.
The infant world, rejoicing, calls out for and seeks
the nurse whom the breeze of the warm sky has given.
The country youth play across the face of the fields,
looking to the sweet burden of their hard labour.
The year creeps on exulting, drawn along through the murmurs of spring,
bringing honey crammed for lips about to speak.
Along with the world, our mind stammers out its songs:
may a golden right hand bring help to beginnings.
The reaper brings the ears more gladly to the sickle
if he keeps combing the crop with the hoe.
Now, teacher, granting them spring, take up the stock of Proculus,
lest too much heat in their studies scorch the tender boys.
Let the laws be kept; let learning run in them as their inheritance does.
Their grandfather surpassed the rivers of Pindar,
he who sang learned songs with the plectrum of the Camenae,
and of whom the choirs of Apollo left nothing unsung.
Phoebus, grown stronger, would soon call him back to his aid,
as the nobility of the art, should Marsyas come again.
4. EPITHALAMIUM SPOKEN FOR MAXIMUS, V.S. PREFACE.
While the year, with the new sun, shapes the tender ears of grain,
Nature sits in the bridal chamber as the world grows warm.
The world is painted with the varied hues of flowers:
the soil wears a single face: grace, adornment, love.
The moist strawberry-trees grow strong in the life-giving warmth,
and the thickened sap nourishes fiery seeds.
The earth rises up, swollen by its wedded spirit;
the swelling wood grows green with wanton spoils.
The grass, suckling in the turf, is pushed up into a knot;
the vine's arms put forth budding fingers.
Across the face of things a law, as bridesmaid, joins the wedding torches:
the breeze of the sky makes every shoot a bridegroom.
So with one desire light, sky, rivers, Nereus,
mountains, meadows and beasts conceive their joys.
From you, Maximus, the world takes the spring it shows,
and your dowry adorns the bounty of nature,
you in whom blood, wealth, talent, mind and wishes stand supreme,
upheld by the foremost brow of the Muses.
Our age has produced you as a monument of faith,
and, matching you in virginity of body and heart,
a pure life gives you a bride who surpasses you in merits,
and when she surpasses you, the palm comes to you that way.
On her snowy lips a kindred flame smiles,
and modest blushes are scattered over her white face.
Be present, I pray, fountain of speech, in mind, voice and plectrum,
art, nature, Muse and Phoebus, by which eloquence swells.
Nothing mean should sound in the praises of the Maximi.
Common words often wear down a lofty head.
Kindly Venus, the world her captive, pouring out
the gifts of flowers, playing through pleasant places,
while she makes the spring with the price and the star
of her shining beauty,
scorned all the glory of a golden robe,
refused the pomp of foreign metal:
richer once adornment was banished, she stood
with her hair let loose.
Whatever dye the noble wool has drunk by art,
prized for its counterfeit colour,
and the little stones of the icy sea as well,
she surpasses naked.
Beneath the sparse and gaping thread there had shone
the jewels of her breast, on rosy nipples.
When she denies her limbs the envious garment,
there is a second light.
She smiled at her body revealed without a cloud;
its prison broken, it shone serene,
and what the ill-guarding garment had kept
is laid open by art.
The winged one was coming back with his bow unstrung,
cursing his quiver, withered with idleness,
slowly carrying arrows
wet with no blood.
Then, his weapons drooping, he addresses his mother thus:
"Mother, we have lost the rewards of our prowess.
Nowhere now does Cytherea's name resound; the tale of the Loves
is laughed at, and there are not offspring enough for the rising age.
A wasting virginity possesses the cold limbs
of many; with new fervour lofty vows
tame the flesh: the world barely survives in name.
Men in their prime imitate the trembling old, and youths the decrepit.
Look: across the boundless fields of the ages the harvest of marriage
is rare; among the flowers only old age,
hungry and pale, puts forth its white hairs.
Their one creed is to be swayed by no sweetness,
and to trample under evil precepts whatever could win over tender hearts;
everywhere a public mourning
is kept; for the chaste it is a crime even to have named the marriage-bed.
You lie there idle and, unaware of such great authority,
gaze, naked, at your limbs through your streaming hair.
Up, come, quickly shake off the sleep that hinders you,
and let it not be thought—a shameful thing—that the laws of chastity,
that ill-counselling law, hold your divinity captive."
At such words even the bowels of the sea would have caught fire.
The golden light gathers her loose hair into a knot,
and, enclosing her natural beauty in a garment,
she changed her appearance. Then whatever the jasper gleams with,
the emerald, shaped as if from pasture, green in its costliness,
and the thing that lies in shells, better than the venom that guards it,
come white, to take on [?] a snowy light from her body.
A splendid mantle narrows over her girded loins,
and a hard girdle pressed in her tender breasts.
She speaks to her son: "Whom, my hope, are you trying to pierce?
Whom are we pursuing? Where do you bid us go? After idleness a greater
flame is fitting: let the peoples learn that the goddess grows
when she lies neglected. Let fires renewed with double care
show that the gods lose nothing by sleep.
Look, you see Maximus, the only hope of a most exalted family,
mocking the sweet torches of marriage through long forgetfulness.
He follows his mother, a woman purer than heaven itself,
who, as we know, rises above womanhood in mind.
He has tamed the boy in himself, inheriting the ways of his forefathers:
to our shame, alas, he has remained unknown to us for a long age.
Let my torch reach his hidden inmost parts:
let him sigh, desire, run to and fro, burn and plead."
So she speaks, and, clasping her offspring in a kindly embrace,
she pressed soft kisses on him with honeyed lips.
He flies off, swimming through the clouds on a swift wind,
uniting all the elements in wanton frenzy.
When he stopped and saw the young man in the crimson of his beauty,
"Do you, puffed up, despise Dione's son?" he said.
"Come here, you who are to worship Venus: the pyre that has caught fire more slowly
burns long and hot, and whatever wood is taken from the pyre
will restore the quick embers."
He drew out the dart with which he had pierced all the gods.
Then the handsome bow bent into a smooth curve:
his arms drew the arrow in opposite directions.
The winged boy's right hand senses the wound in advance by touch,
and soon he strikes, hailing the deed with a joyful shout:
"I am the one (why do you tremble?) who, though always scorned, have clung
to your vitals, runaway. With this victim we make offering
to my mother, whom you have not looked up to for many years."
Then again, having searched for a girl born of a great line
to join to him in marriage, he sees the girl's lofty
star-like beauty and, astonished, turned his eyes to his mother,
thinking her his sister; he praises the noble theft.
But the boy strikes the tender girl with a gentler arrow,
and spent the full force of the stronger blow on the man.
After this, as he leaves, he soothes their hearts with words:
"Young man, let our wounds strengthen your powers.
For whoever is struck by my point increases.
These wars, believe me, produce many grandchildren.
Be happy, and always carry my gifts with you."
Now, nobles, set me, aided by Pierian favour,
among glad things with joyful brow.
Let those who by their kindness make a slender poet learned
sustain him through the whole song.
The talent that frosts now oppress,
may spring expand, reviving it with warmth.
5. A JOURNEY.
Nurturer of talent, fountain of speech, abundance of tongue,
let the Castalian water come, with which Thracian Orpheus
kindled shipwrecked hearts with its outpoured stream.
Let it be present and close the cracks of a parched heart.
I am about to tell of the waters of the Eridanus; unless with a broad stream
I drench my dry limbs with Pegasean liquid,
parched words will barely drip from a starved account.
Supply me, water, that I may tell of the heaped-up waves.
How well he describes the waters to whom the river murmurs pleasantly!
It was the season of the year when the vine-shoot flourishes with mellow grapes
and sets out the gifts of autumn across the world,
when Lyaeus, his robe soaked with rains from outside,
stretches the grapes' tunics, the prison of the must.
The law of its banks overcome by abundant rains,
the Po had then by chance covered the captive fields;
they were white with foam, with swollen and threatening backs.
The rooftops of farmhouses still standing ran through the waves.
The flood then set the roof it had snatched upon the shore,
and though the land was changed, the cottages' fortune survived.
You would have seen woods, bidden to lose their place,
hurrying, with the Po as their guide, to the devouring flames.
Then I, drawn by burning love for my sister,
whose son the Fates had cut down with cruel thumb
and taken away, leaving her house bereaved though her husband lived—
the Fates whom Avernus bore for ever-lasting turmoil [?]—
chose to risk even my life to comfort her.
That ruler of the Ligurians, greatest of rivers,
brought under the yoke, groaned beneath the weight of the boat;
he swelled, and then put aside his threats and blasts,
and he who had conquered the heavens was bidden to yield to me alone.
So does piety tame the elements, so does it restrain all things
for one whose mind is held by compassion pleasing to God.
Look, again the sky, covered with wet clouds,
drew up waters with which, rushing down, it might drown every field.
The shipwrecked earth did not see the face of heaven,
and the darkness, bereft of stars, flashed dreadfully.
The fish wandered into houses, though not as a captive,
and the people of the river licked up food across the tables.
The flood spewed out the deep inner rooms of men's homes,
and watery expanses closed over fields that had been dust.
Having come through the first, I saw the dangers return.
That triumphant one, a raw recruit for the contests of Nereus,
I carried a cold heart through the liquid waters
and looked with dry eyes on the anger of the sea;
when suddenly the old local saw the flood swallowed up,
he laughed at the signs that remained of the fear he had cast off.
The rich fields gleamed with mingled metal,
and the Eridanus shone, adorned with bright sands.
A glad boatman at once took me into his alder boat,
to whom his cargo had long since given a happy omen.
Unskilled, he steered the helm, kept safe by his burden,
and with Christ as guide carried me to festive shores.
6. SPEECH OF ENNODIUS THE DEACON WHEN HE RETURNED FROM ROME.

Cheerfulness is always a friend to a man returning to his native soil, since he trusts that he has escaped the fears which his anxious mind bred while he was abroad, as though they had been foreordained and arranged by an oppressive heaven. A serene voice of gladness is therefore owed, lest silent joys take on the look of grief. For to whom does the secret of a mind exiled [?] amid such great matters lie open, unless it is unlocked by the key of the mouth? The Mantuan declared that even swans, on their return, play with their wings. What am I to do, caught in the middle of a sheer drop, I who owe to my return the faithful duty of speaking, and to my calling the necessity of silence? Step aside for a while, I beg you, censure of a weightier office: you have never mixed yourself with joys at the right moment. The most illustrious of the prophets, bringing their words under the law of verse, sang their longings and their prayers in song; hearts dedicated to converse with God distributed the laws of the Church among the peoples with the plectrum. Why should I, still in the infancy of rank and merit, not strive to emulate the deeds of the greatest, especially since the image of such narration strengthens the soldier of the altar to meet the wars that arise against the faith? Nor will I hesitate to say what is established by a present example. We have already learned with what whirling force the spear must be hurled for love of the faith, and no mean conflict has raised us to the reward and titles of valour. I will gladly tell my joys, then, in a musical style, and I promise, with God's help, to proclaim their fulfilment with the mightiest trumpets of eloquence. The venom of barking tongues will assail me, but I will add to the exercises of my profession and my talent whatever the slanderer has heaped up against the merit of the accused. It is the habit of a brightly shining conscience to add the bites of rivals to the profit of its reputation, and to hunt out gains of fame from the envious. Wickedly persistent tooth of envy, break; and you who seek kindling for abuse in the very place of glory, be silent. Tell me where reward comes to merit from, if you count it as boasting that we please by our own sweat. Toil is the friend of learning and joined to religion by a kind of kinship. Just as moist grafts, wedded to foreign stocks, give the branches a nobility of fruit that the seedlings, for all their bearing, had long not known, so a man endowed with liberal training raises a mind pregnant with good care to the hope of a better yield. The poisons of schemes prepared for the deaths of men are driven from the soul, and the moisture of deadly sap is done away with whenever minds give themselves to occupations of this kind. From here, for those who move on to brighter things, the secrets of the daily [?] books lie open; and when the understanding unlocks their door to him who knocks, it makes a road once unknown passable for the peoples under its guidance, as it leads the fastidious on by the splendour of its eloquence, and the less learned by a crafted Latinity and, as they say, an artful rusticity. Who would not love such a guide to salvation, who would not follow him, who by mixing the sweet with the necessary and the severe with the sweet compels even the unwilling to love and to desire the teachings of life? But of this another time. Let the honourable aims of the task I have begun be fulfilled. We speak among those who know the world: it is a matter of virtue to contain joy, and of a second kind of diligence to display it along the worked path of brilliant diction—above all today, when a part of myself, having crossed the threshold of eloquence, gives his parent through exultation the eloquence that talent denies, since the occasion grants what nature has not supplied. Well done, young man of outstanding virtues, who in the white blossom already show the number of the fruits. You enable me to drive off the ice of affliction, and you invite me to the springtime of speech. For while I spend on gladness what you owe to your studies, I think we both make progress. For it is much the same thing to train a beginner and to call one already idle back to the passion for declamation.
After hoary winters, after the losses of the icy deep,
whenever the sailor takes a calm course,
he grieves and despairs of fair weather from the faithless sea,
and does not believe the face he sees is the sea's.
A light breeze whistles; he fears mighty storms,
and judges even gentle waves to be threats.
If the Zephyrs ripple the sails hanging from the mast
and the breath of wind plays in sweet compliance,
he swears that nature, thrown into confusion by the winds, is losing its laws,
and believes that ancient chaos is at hand.
So in calm times the fear of danger takes away joy:
there is no whole trust either in glad times or in doubtful ones.
Not otherwise has Rome returned those she held in various perils
to the bosom of the longed-for shore.
They soothe the venerable power of the sea with song,
because the hooked anchor bites into its own soil.
But the breezes that should bring soft sleep to the weary
trouble the mind of the soldier of the sea.
He masters the ship's gear, plies the oars and shakes out the sails:
so the mind suffers the shipwreck of suspicion.
Let him come who trod the blue waters with dry feet
(for he will be the harbour of salvation for the weary),
who bound the waters and poured the rock into cups,
who loosened stones and made waters solid,
whom his mother, made fruitful without seed, brought forth for the ages,
joining to motherhood the burden of virginity,
who overcame death by the gift of his own death,
giving the world the life he brought forth by dying:
may he look on me with favour from high heaven.
Then may I reach my homeland, then the help of a harbour.
Though the unleashed winds sweep the cloudy seas,
they will strike my leaky ship without doing harm.
Then I shall beat sweet drums, with strings in tune,
and paint my songs with fresh flowers.
To confess it, the learned agree that a glad man speaks well:
the sad hearts of a verse-maker achieve nothing.
But let spring return, and let the winter of fear now end.
Bind leafy garlands to wreathe my hair:
let me sing the beautiful songs that the bard Ambrose used to utter
while he fed his people with his mouth.
7. PREFACE TO FAUSTUS.

Had I not learned that the serenity of your conscience abjures the scabby itch of this evil, I would declare a richness of eloquence hateful to me. Let a thing friendly to treachery keep away from good deeds. Yet I declare that your caution has done me harm. Until now you have withheld from the dryness of my poor little talent the rain that nourishes fruit. Good God, how clearly I see that the resources of speech in me are foreign, acquired from the riches of your mouth! It belongs to wealthy speech, as far as I can tell, to polish with the file of skill tongues that are rusty and minds that are dull. You share a kind of partnership with the Maker of men: he fashioned from nothing, you restore to something better. I give thanks for the poem I have received, though I grieve that the kindness was delayed. Yet, to the disgrace of the Camenae, who are never without a Gluvidenus, I have added verses and, as the saying goes, I have lavishly not spared paper that is going to perish anyway. Read poems that will stir up merriment, and hold back, as they say, the astonishing ornaments of a familiar evil.
In the middle of a river, Faustus, you set the innards on fire,
whose wave of song feeds a mighty thirst.
Who could bear the heat of these waters, and drink down with parched mouth
the flames that are kin to their streams?
Your words breed a steaming heat from their very spring:
the cups supply what sets the liver burning.
Whoever hurries to the river of genius,
let him be in no doubt: he drinks only to thirst the more.
A noble water has seasoned it with a hidden savor;
let him reckon the loss as well, [?] though I carry away less from it.
Let no glib tongue, trusting in the Attic buskin,
boast to the old man of the ancients' nobility.
Faustus composes new songs after the manner of the ancients,
and with skill he carves his melody into its members.
Taught to bring unwrought words back to the anvil,
he tests three and four times every verse he makes.
Hoary antiquity tells that Myron with his fingers gave breath
to the work he shaped with his life-giving hand.
You give a face with words, and limbs with rhythm:
what nature grants to God, your studies grant to you.
If with your skill you turned your plectrum upon an aged corpse,
your building lyre would make it young again.
If you feigned flowers along the wain of icy Boötes,
soon a breeze would whistle springtime tunes about the Bear.
Let the snowy wilds bear roses, let the frosts pour you new wine,
let Pallas bring her gifts beneath the burning star;
let the fish swim across the airy heights to which you carry it;
if you command it in verse, the stag falls in love with the marble sea.
From the very jaws, from the unfed belly, with mighty mouth
you could snatch the prey the lion holds in its mouth.
Now I know where you have dragged me, you loves of Castalia:
your gifts are added to my faults.
My stitched-together skiff is swept toward swelling storms,
to suffer the winter south winds — a skiff which a poor sailor,
shaping a leaky hull from thin bark,
put together and gave, without praise, the name of 'bean-pod.'
It has never known the Aegean sea, nor the shores of Phrixus,
nor any of the seas that fierce Aeolus can sweep up from the bottom;
but, very cautious, it skirts the calm bays
of the deep flood, where the South Wind serves,
not where he seeks to rule, whenever, as the oars move slowly there,
the breeze whistles as it runs across the trembling keel.
For while the linen sails, bound to the topmost yards, ripple,
the blasts that bring death to others bring me sleep.
Here I will turn my stern, entrusting my canvas to steady winds,
the courses of my art and my resources.
Bend the course of the sails and the helm toward the shore, Phoebus:
let the hooked anchor bite into the furrowed ground.
Muse, chief of the finest sayings,
weaving the grassy crown of ivy
which you bestow on accomplished poets,
bind my hair.
The keel furrows the boundless sea;
my hand knows not how to reach the helm with skill,
where the friend of art calls for deft steering
through the waves.
You are going to Faustus, the scales of speech,
whose eloquence is as vast as the deep,
whom the world reveres as more brilliant
than light itself.
He holds the balance of the ear among the Muses;
his blade cuts out every wound,
whatever lies hidden in the inmost marrow
of a sickly poem.
If he would weigh my modest dithyrambs
with the mind by which he governs the whole world,
amid the commonplace babbling of infants,
that is praise.
Faustus, my light,
my hope and salvation,
this small gift
of humble letters
receive with gladness.
So may Christ on high
keep your offspring
shining.
Stretch out your right hand,
you of kindly name.
Pleasing to the Thunderer
is the grain-offering of the pious.

VIII. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS. PREFACE. The country shepherd does not lay aside his pipe whenever he looks upon his rustic flock. Silent groves breed a fearful solitude, and dread is everywhere when no sound is heard to comfort the wilderness. But if the leafy crowns of the trees counterfeit the semblance of a tongue in the whistling of the breezes, and a pleasant rustling addresses the man with the laughing motion of the leaves, he will think himself among companies thronging at his side; and he whom nature herself addresses in his solitude through any of her elements bemoans no hardship. Then he delights to put to his lips the pipe, companion of his exile, and with breaths scattered through the holes of its shell to compose some measure out of breath and air. Then with rough, unpolished tongue he hails his Palaemon; then he counts how many night-watches are needed to guard the folds; then he sighs over the manifold ambushes of wolves, sharpened by their teacher, hunger; then whatever he has breathed out falls into speech: in its company he strives to console himself, to soothe himself. If, while he is so occupied, someone skilled should bring him a cithara that converses through its strings, and some mocking city man should offer him those talkative strings, his naked simplicity is in doubt which to choose, since the touch of the lyre, even under wandering fingers, gives back a sweet sound such as can break the soul. Yet he thinks it a sin if, drawn by the charm of another's pursuit, he should learn not to love his ancestral skill; for while unbridled ambition does not measure the bounds of rustic learning, he knows that in longing for higher things he will lose even what lies within his power, when the nursling of the huts, not knowing what he is worth, scorns as something foreign the very modesty of his father's training. Not otherwise, most distinguished man, you who are to be counted among the greatest stars of the senate, radiance of eloquence, flame of talent, splendor of oratory, treasury of diction — not otherwise do humbly told things delight me in the trackless groves, like a shepherd's pipe, as I fear your cithara and praise the plectrum which, as I have woven above, you, a man of the city, bring to my rustic fingers. Remove, I beg you, the lure of polished speech that you employ to invite me. Away with the bonds of conversation that you use even among the learned. Restrain the fingers of your words, with which you are accustomed to drive the souls of the reluctant to your wishes. Let me either cover my ignorance with silence or bring a commonplace song to others on a screeching straw: to converse with you is a thing of long-standing merit and of new good fortune. But if, forgetful of myself, I attempt it, having seized the chariot of the sun against [?], I justly undergo the fate of Phaethon. And since the talk has touched on him and taken the form of a warning, the poem below shows what must be done.
Fame reports — who knows not how to lose the deeds of the ancients,
who always tells whatever has been in the world —
that while Titan scattered the seeds of Light across the sky
and enriched the world with noble rays,
while wet reins held in the steaming four-horse team
and the flood sent forth the shining day everywhere,
the Sun guided the rippling reins with skilled hands,
and the light, knowing him well, bore its masterly lord.
But after, at Phaethon's pleading, he resolved
to hand over his kingdom without testing the youth's strength,
the star felt from the first movements a driver unworthy of his line,
and, the horses having thrown him, began to run wild.
Then the steeds, breathing all their light from their nostrils,
no longer kept the fixed times of their law.
Splendor turned to flame; what it lights, it burned;
and what gives life to the lands brought forth destruction.
Then too, while it shattered the Hyperborean ice with its torch,
the Tanais ran dry, its waters drunk up.
The crystal melted, but the river's course burned:
what dissolved stones bound up the Eridanus.
So I, attempting to run the path of rhetoric,
lay hands on the sun's chariot and its dominion.
I know not what to spend on the star's various regions,
I know not what to hold to: the heat overpowers everything.
The mighty senate shaped you polished to the fingertip
and bade you bring light to its fathers.
You restore Phoebus: for you a fat victim smokes,
for which the gods of heaven would have surrendered their thunderbolt.
But to me my poor gardens can scarcely send
a vegetable that the red clay pot, once it receives it, would refuse.
I am, I confess, one whose words trickle out in the telling,
showing the leanness of a poor talent.
I sing no songs, nor when I play the Muses' measures
will any lasting 'bravo' be granted me by the applauding thumb.
Whatever I once spoke with Apollo's plectrum, I have given up,
forgetting the tongue the strings once gave me.
My rustic right hand wanders over the tender strings;
a barbarous plectrum shatters sweet measures.
Ah, how often on Helicon's glassy grass flowed
the water that smiles upon the lips and makes them thirst!
Ah, how often, my temples wreathed with ivy, I led the dance,
soothing the Aonian assembly with song!
But now through the woods, among the dens of wild beasts,
resolved to wage a rustic campaign,
I commit great seeds to the sturdy furrows,
so that the tares may abandon the seed of life.
Lest milky words lay bare a slackened mind,
and I be called soft in speech and in talent,
let not my tongue run loose across the open plains,
nor let me utter manly words with heavy trumpets;
lest my heart be inflamed by the loud-sounding buskin
and I, a father, grow swollen in my writings and my character.
What harbor, then, for me? The reader seeks fame on every side;
but a steady modesty is truly one's own, if I keep silent.
You may hold the heavens; leave me in peace on earth,
I who know only this: that I have learned nothing well.

IX. AN ADDRESS DELIVERED ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF THE HOLY AND MOST BLESSED BISHOP EPIPHANIUS, IN THE THIRTIETH YEAR OF HIS PRIESTHOOD. PREFACE. I perceive what many are silently saying in their thoughts, and, with the ear of my heart applied, I understand the voice of the heart. For these silences cry out: what does a man of another profession want with such a theme? What does one marked with the titles of humility want with the applause of voices, catching it from the crowds of the common people, clattering as usual — applause stirred up by the popular breeze from the swelling bubbles of partisans? Such things, they say, ought to have been composed long ago, when the flattering flowers of youth, and boyhood still in him, and the slaves of worldly license were smiling [?]; when it was fitting to be carried away by resounding acclamations; when he could be captured even by the outward show of painted pleasure. Why now should he recite in public, whom public praise neither befits nor delights? Let them remember that I am performing a duty of my office, since it is established that in the praises of a bishop I feel what I owe. Though now in untimely praises I render him only modest things, yet hereafter I shall owe him the greatest, for in his service it is best to spend whatever I am able. At the same time I also realized that if an account must be rendered for idle speech, no less must it be rendered for idle silence. For it would be an idle silence if, when the minds of people of every kind around me were rejoicing, I alone withheld words when I could give them — since even in the worship of heaven it is fitting to offer hymns, and we believe that the Lord, who is beyond humanity, is soothed by the pure praises of men and claims this by a special right from those to whom he has given a tongue. What will the bishop do, who by his own prayers brought it about that I am able? For it is written: The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know when I ought to speak a word. Now, I judge, it is fitting, and at the time for speaking the door of the heart is opened. But I will not now open my mouth in poetic praises. Far from me be the bilge-water of verse, which, as it does not praise what is true, so is not itself truly praised. Now grant your favorable attention to one who will speak of certain things. And so, if through the smallness of my talent I say less than the deeds deserve, at least I will not out of boastfulness invent greater things.
For the ancient poets the greatest power of speech
was this: to know how to deceive with learned words.
Praise lay in composing a lying song in praise.
Then fraud was suited to the work; for, after the poet's fashion,
holding fast to what carries guilt, they forbade themselves out of shame
to speak the truth, and faith everywhere despised their song.
An art found favor that befits a crime; for a more learned error
wrung out fearsome poems from practiced tongues.
A law taught them to speak without law, since by art it claims
whatever the laws forbid to be spoken: as restraints upon morals
they fashioned sordid deities in deceitful song;
they spoke of Phoebus and of the thrice-three sisters,
of the Castalian spring, and of Pallas' various arts;
then they told of the laurel, the tripods, the cauldron, the timbrels, the plectrum:
understanding fled them from the path of truth,
and a phantom mocked their wandering efforts.
Now, O faith, spurn the tongue of the lyre that sings
by the mouth of the thumb; rather come now, I pray, you, that Spirit,
by whom, in an unfailing year, is ever revived
whatever the earth creates, the sea begets, the sky brings forth;
who spreads out the seas and gives solid body to the sands,
who stirs the rocks at his command, whom the crag-bristling Caucasus
fears, when through the attentive ear he tames
the strong hearts of his servant; who sees all things, before whom all things tremble:
Fountain, Way, Right Hand, Stone, Calf, Lion, Morning Star, Lamb,
Door, Hope, Power, Word, Wisdom, Prophet,
Victim, Shoot, Shepherd, Mountain, Net, Dove,
Flame, Giant, Eagle, Bridegroom, Patience, Worm,
Son, Most High, Lord, God — Christ, who is all things.
Him I pray to be present to my words, he who, entering the breast
of the ancient prophet in the time of King Pharaoh,
helped the prophet who was to speak with a feeble voice.
He himself was amazed, I think, well aware of his own mouth
and his habitual stammer, as he filled the prince's ears
with weight, voice, sound, sense, uprightness, modesty.
You, holy one, you admonish your servant: grant me to pay the thanks
that it is a joy to owe. Behold, we all embrace
the holy day on which a radiance chose to set itself upon the earth
more readily, and to quicken souls with its nearby rays —
a day in which the world rejoices, though these are not the world's joys.
Do you see it adoring, lowering its trembling face
in homage to the bishop? It senses the festive season
of his birthday, nor, though sad for its lost children, does it scorn it.
This day was for all the cause of life and of salvation,
loosing the bonds of the ancient sin.
On it Christ granted an ornament and a defense to the Ausonian
lands, one to govern the peoples with an even mind
and rule the nations with piety; for them the author of Olympus,
as he had promised, has provided a king of like uprightness,
just as God himself, propitious, gives laws from his gleaming throne.
He whose mind is conscious of the right will always be
next to heaven — he whom just men approve, whom, with the world as judge,
the public prayers choose. I confess, great were the votes
it bestowed, that he might enjoy the bosom of a see not bought.
A free multitude set you over itself as lord for ever,
a multitude to be praised for its servitude. Oh, how great
was the fervor everywhere! As the holy tumult of the world applauded,
all had one mind, all the crowds one voice.
Yet they strove to outdo one another in their wishes,
as if they had cause to fight hand to hand
with a dread enemy: then the common people conquer with their own blood,
whenever they have pledged themselves to endure dangers.
Not otherwise does the Caspian tigress, with young, circle Niphates
or train her cubs in the work of seizing prey;
she rages against the absent, and with savage spirit chews
mortal limbs, and seeks the death of men with bloody mouth.
One marveled at the ripe age of his mind in tender years;
another boasted of his parents of ancient stock;
another, whose mind was little content with blood,
recalls a thousand worthy pedigrees of the man's virtues:
with what praise do titles then stand out
whenever they are surpassed, and the glory of character
brings forth for the vanquished a famous triumph through long ages!
Another carries to heaven with praises the chastity that blooms
the more beautiful in a beautiful body, and the form
smiling with chaste light; that face indeed brought him
honor, which for many has often been a cause
of danger: it is enough for the beautiful to have remained chaste.
Such things are given only from the highest summit of Olympus.
If anywhere the advantages of beauty fall to holy minds
or grow in them, then men strive to conquer themselves
in war, and the right hand of the soul pours out beauty and the gifts of earth,
and lives for itself while it dies to that.
While the people told these things with many mouths,
all the throngs held one fixed judgment.
The company of priests and the venerable senate of the age
chose, willed, deserved, received, loved him.
But see, I had passed over another thing, new to tell and wondrous to all,
at which everyone trembles, which the world looks up to.
He was scarcely in his first years, when the threshold of light
is trodden with tottering feet, when from those snatched
from the mother's breast the sweeter nourishment is withdrawn from the tender draught,
when the stern mother, perhaps, cunningly pours the counterfeit taste
of herbs upon the complaining little lips,
so that the child may not know its mother by taste,
and so, the milk being refused, a prepared poison
is sucked down by unaccustomed throats through a laughable trick.
Such was his age when the sign occurred.
For they say his cradle shone with a great
light, since such splendor had flashed about him
as the sky could then pour out in service,
when, commanded to serve a man, the swift fire of Olympus
lifts his mortal limbs in a sudden ascent,
imitating the rapid course of hoofed horses:
not otherwise did the favoring flame then, roaming over the boy,
circle, illuminate, revere, look up to, and encompass him.
Then the awestruck father, with lowered eyes, spoke:
"Highest of gods, guardian of the holy, who from heaven's summit
make favorable omens, which you behold with a favoring eye,
this child I give to you from his first, still crawling years,
holy Father, [?] one whom not yet, with the snares of their craft,
have the slippery ages entangled in earthly faults.
Nor may they ever: let him be, highest God, a rich gift to you."
So he spoke, and shed the tears that joy brings forth.
From there he gladly seeks out Crispinus, whom it is not granted
to describe with worthy eloquence — not even if he should now rise from Avernus
who could draw the forests from the stiff rocks of the Apennines
to his plectrum while the rivers stood still.
He was rather an Elijah: for who else would leave an Elisha
on earth, with a doubled gift of the palm?
He nourished him with the holy milk that Paul pressed
from the breast, he whose right hand is full of the Gospel's breasts.
Hail, holy father; hail for ever, ashes
of Crispinus, received into heaven, to whose credit overflows
whatever we admire as worthy in this man of Christ's teaching.
You, his heir, rightly possess the wealth handed down to you.
No small matter proves it, joined with tripled talents:
it shows the captive multitude recalled from the regions
of the western world, which suppliant Gaul sends back.
Savage hearts, having seen you, learned to bend;
you overcame an armed king with prayers, greatest one.
So the fighter blunts swords with the lash of the tongue,
so the strong blade of words storms the iron.
For if those who compare the greatest things with small may speak what is permitted,
so the steward awaits his lord when the fields are tamed,
when with the tooth of the curved hoe he marks out
the well-softened fields, and so combs the face of the soil with ploughs
that the running vintage foams over the brimming vats.
He grafts foreign plants onto a strange turf;
the newcomer tree is joined in close-knit bonds;
the stocks are cut back, and he weds the shoot cut with the knife
to the stem; the wood is bitten with a tender cleft;
a nobility not its own rises from a small bud;
the scion grows together, rich with an unfamiliar gift,
as he joins the moistened slips to new bark.
Likewise he paints the beds with Paestan roses;
the field is clothed in a rustic yet royal purple.
Lilies are poured out in place of gleaming whitewash;
then he paints violets, clover, colocasia, marigolds,
cinnamon, thyme, narcissi, balsam, costus.
Then he sows the seeds the reborn phoenix carries.
This servant the lord, on his arrival, bids recline at table,
and he himself rises and serves the dishes with his own hands.
So, cultivator of souls, through thirty years
your fields breathe the scent of roses, and, broken in upon by no
frosts, the soil does not wither, for the teacher keeps it in perpetual spring
with the fragrant turf of merits.
Whenever your arbutus trees grow dry for want of dew,
you water them with tears, and heap there too a basket
of unclean dung: then the tree rises with rich branches,
then, fruitful for God, it rises above the laws of its birth.
Receive now with favor, golden light of our life,
the modest song that joy makes me bring forth for you.
When God has advanced my wishes in the order begun,
and the docile vine-shoot your right hand is planting has shone forth,
I will repay you what I owe more strongly a hundred years hence.
Lo, I have resolved to carve for you now such a song as I could,
father, under a knotty law, which a rule close to punishment
has bound with art in measures of varied kind,
so that nowhere might a deceitful syllable falter. I have spoken.
X. EVENING HYMN.
Now, covered with a darkening cloak,
the earth receives the night,
so that, through a sweet death,
living bodies may regain their strength.
A gentler image of death
brings near the tomb of sleep,
while the mind, panting from the heat of day,
cools in rest.
Christ, Light, Life, Truth,
let not the dark hours of sleep,
furnished with gloomy shadows,
summon us to darkness.
Let no night make us its subjects
beneath the covering of black night,
nor let drunken heat
paint false bodies,
dealing out real guilt
to those unaware of a false crime;
but you, through the gifts of rest,
stand by us, ever-wakeful guardian.
Let the cunning enemy be far away;
let whatever harms, sleep.
He who with savage tooth
strives to devour those lying in their beds,
let him, bound hand and foot, lament
that he has assailed those you cherish.
Let not the spirit be shipwrecked
and slain in the sodden flesh.
Let chastity adorn the bed,
chastity that shines first among the virtues;
let faith live in the breast,
faith that blooms in everlasting light.
XI. HYMN FOR A TIME OF SORROW.
God, everlasting joy,
Christ, peace of the anxious heart
and harbor of the storm-tossed,
whom no tempest, even should it
sweep the depths with turbulent motion,
can drive from the heart;
you who raise up what is sunk in the sea,
who raise what is weighed down by burdens,
who, guide of the shipwrecked prophet
while he lived as food for the monster,
while the sea knew not what it held,
as one demanding payment, snatched its meal
unharmed from the beast's throat.
Brought back by a dreadful oarsman,
kept safe by the worst of guardians,
the prophet, having proclaimed you as God,
then carried out your commands more boldly.
The beast had carried him, fasting,
through foul tombs in loathsome waters:
living, he endured the sepulchre,
the meal of a living urn.
He revealed the secrets of the whale,
a revered witness of its inmost parts.
So we pray you, King and God:
snatch us, broken with grief, as food
from the belly of our cares.
What kills us lives in our marrow;
the depths of our inward parts are in turmoil.
In the wellspring of the flesh there is a burning
that drowns, scorches, and afflicts;
but if you look upon us serenely,
affliction will give birth to joy.
XII. HYMN OF ST CYPRIAN.
Of Cyprian, prophet and martyr,
the heart, tongue, mind, and dignity
are made known by his enduring death:
slaughter gave him a life-giving tomb;
a light born of the sword shines forth.
He was resplendent in his words
and rich in a matchless eloquence,
the wave of a torrential flood,
overcoming the darts hurled against the horn
with ready speech —
he who rightly rendered to Christ
the riches of a revered heart.
Now he fulfills his former office:
as advocate he pleads and wins,
softens harsh sentences in their cases,
makes the guilty blessed,
breaking sins with his chant.
Neither flame, prison, nor chain
can harm those whom he aids.
Ordered to sacrifice victims,
he laughed at the pitiable gods;
then, as danger pressed upon him,
he escaped danger by death:
with a turn of speech
he dismissed the short delays before the blows,
summoned the swords more gladly,
swifter than death as it ran upon him.
Maximus the proconsul
could not be crueler,
since what he threatens is a gift;
nor does a gentler anger delay
those who long to see Christ.
XIII. HYMN FOR PENTECOST.
And this is a gift from on high,
that one tongue campaigns in every tongue.
Who would not proclaim the Thunderer's rewards
through the gifts of that same Lord?
He who is wise brings it about by speaking
that the speaker speaks words worthy of God.
Behold, the Spirit pours himself in
and once more equips mouths.
He enters hearts long torpid,
now cleared of their cloud.
On this day, for the apostles,
while the Word divides words,
mighty over the world in speech,
he also brought together the hearts of the world.
Let him be borne up with highest praise:
one man has the mouths of the nations;
Thracian, Gaul and Indian are one.
What charming Greece speaks in play,
the fierce, barbarous
shrieking of Canopus' muttering speech,
what the Parthian tongue barks out,
has filled the breasts of the strangers.
Men run toward the world's salvation,
against the world's will, by as many ways
as the holy release
of Easter grace now presses on,
while it adorns the mystic crown
with its sevenfold gift.
Increases of fullness
supply wealth to the rich.
Now sing psalms with mind and voice:
this our mind owes to God.
14. HYMN OF ST STEPHEN.
What is mightier than Stephen?
Say "Crown": he is a martyr.
The man is what the reward is:
his name is the fruit of his labor.
This brief praise becomes ample
if the illustrious are so named.
Look: the minister of slaughter,
bestowing life out of death,
gives to salvation what he denies.
Happy beneath these blows,
he becomes everlasting through his end.
With his blood he prepares light,
and heaven by the gift of the tomb,
so that triumph may put the enemy to flight:
he joins battle as if for the palm.
He was the first to enter the road
that no steps had yet trodden.
He surveyed the secrets of heaven
and, still hidden in the garment of flesh,
cried out: "Behold, the Son
stands at the Father's right hand."
While the wicked hurled stones,
while they brought a thousand engines of death,
he alone, conscious of good,
prayed, speaking out of faith,
that the wrath of heaven might not destroy
the guilty in their ignorance:
let their madness go unpunished.
Rage had brought the accused forward,
but his toil ran on in prayers:
the executioner groaned at the torment
of the one he had subdued, as that one grew greater.
15. HYMN OF ST AMBROSE.
Ambrose is borne to heaven
by his name, his honor and his deeds.
He owes nothing to eloquence;
his every endowment comes from his character.
Strong, he wants no helper,
protected by his own shield.
In the flesh, nothing of the flesh rules him:
the mind, queen in the body,
has shattered every slippery lust.
So he lived not for himself
but wholly for God his maker.
Hence, added to the apostles,
he brought back the faith that had been driven out,
and told the triumphs of the martyrs
with the laurels of a flourishing tongue.
With his mouth he snatched the prey
from the jaws of the savage serpent.
He who fights the wars of Christ
is feared by swords though he is unarmed.
Buried, he lives and helps,
holding the helm of the Church.
Justina lost her venom;
punishment gives the prophet his reward.
Remember your see, O light;
adorn, holy one, your successors,
upheld by a noble founder,
so that the leader on the serene height
may not shudder, covered in cloud —
he who is shepherd of bishops,
who drives away all that darkens,
who governs the flock of princes,
and is master of teachers.
16. HYMN ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD.
Now Christ has ascended to heaven.
He first put death to death;
buried, he drove out destruction:
death falls at death's onslaught.
Sing the deed, you ages:
his burial subdued Tartarus;
slain, he conquered his end.
Pale fate therefore mourns
where it had presumed to rejoice.
The devourer is caught by the bait;
the plunderer of all is now the prey.
Now he is led away bound in a net,
he lies in the coils of a chain;
the serpent has spat out his poisons.
The meek one tramples pride,
the Lamb disembowels the lion.
This is a greater show of power,
that you, Christ, take on what is ours
and, hidden in a servant's garment,
carry us forward to triumph,
than if from your glittering throne
you terrified the guilty with lightning.
God lies open through all things,
withdrawn behind no covering;
but to raise up those who lie fallen,
deigning to be what we are,
he himself redeemed what was rightfully his.
He brought the lost sheep back
into the shepherd's keeping.
Lift up the gates, you angels:
the dread Judge enters,
greater for his trophies won from the enemy.
17. HYMN OF ST EUPHEMIA.
What tongue could, what pen would be strong enough
to tell the triumphs of so great a virgin?
[?] learn, you men who are soft of mind:
she offers an example — take it, you idle ones —
when a brave girl overcomes men.
Virtue never knows softness,
nor do the laws of sex or a broken spirit belong to her
who has once conceived Christ in her heart.
Those in whose minds God is stored
free their hearts from perishable chains.
With her body she wore out mighty torments:
as punishment grew weary, love of the cross grew.
If you could know how a martyr conquers,
mad torturer, you would learn to spare.
Flames, scourge, executioners, wheels —
she who must follow the cross does not greatly fear them.
When, with furnaces crackling with fire,
she is said to have been ordered thrown headlong
by Priscus, more harmful than a fountain of poison
(for so, in that foul time,
they named the deadly judge of the holy virgin),
while his ministers eagerly longed
to give the martyr as food to the furnace,
a light then, more serene than the light of Olympus,
thwarted the cruel work of those who willed it,
when those who bore the sword declared with one voice:
"Rather, we pray, send us from here to Tartarus,
for our hand will not violate the holy one."
His liver swells, burning with gall;
soon stones, pits, lashes, beasts —
and, a greater poison, he prepares blandishments,
which the heroic maiden bravely withstood.
18. HYMN OF ST NAZARIUS.
The narrow seasons of life,
confined within small bounds,
a holy death allows to grow:
it makes their ends eternal.
From the harvest of deaths comes
that by which the human race may rise:
Nazarius, of good stock,
added light out of death.
Blessed in the reign of Nero,
having endured many evils,
he traveled the world, not chilled
by heavy fear of heart;
but to instill in the unbelieving
the path by which they might climb to heaven,
a true teacher, he gave examples
by his deeds, not by words.
For that leader is brave
who teaches war by his own strength.
What soldier do words draw on
if the general holds back from action?
The windy exhortation of the tongue
lacks what example supplies.
But after he had poured great seeds
back into the best clods,
as the hoe wrote upon the earth,
he soon made for Milan,
where, in a noble triumph,
he thrust back the ruin of the flesh.
Lying in an unworthy resting place,
he soon, awe-inspiring, admonishes the bishop,
so that, restored once more to the world,
he might add bright gifts anew.
19. HYMN OF ST MARY.
To speak of the virgin who bore a child,
what is worthy of Mary's praise?
Let the birth supply it, adorn it, demand it;
what the closed gate and what the open gate
require, let her herself suggest.
Let the words be like the miracle:
why, my mind, do you look for order?
Nature has lost everything;
our salvation is that we are overcome.
While the virgin lived alone,
she conceived a son through her ear,
a deed done while her body stood amazed:
her womb swells by the Spirit.
What the tongue cast forth is the seed;
the Word is bound within flesh.
From his mother he is wholly ours;
from his Father, God, differing in nothing:
the offspring is whole for both,
for him who begets and for her who receives.
He is no greater than his servants,
nor yet does he become less than his Begetter.
The sealed fountain receives words,
the sealed fountain brings forth limbs:
no narrow crack gave way,
and yet a true offspring springs forth.
Tell me, mother and virgin, I pray:
does anyone close the door as he goes out?
Wombs are strained by what they bear;
this son is the very bond of chastity.
(You who) are believed more worthy of Christ's praise
than the beings above,
remember us, mighty one.
20. HYMN OF ST MARTIN.
When I speak of Martin's deeds,
I pass over nothing worthy of praise:
the virtue divided among all,
gathered together, has shown forth one man.
By great toil he is a martyr,
with the spirit victorious over the flesh:
this comes nearest to triumphs,
if one tramples down the wars within.
When the body loses its strength,
the victory stands secure in its laurels:
he exalts the enemy of souls
who does the bidding of his limbs.
Though he did not yet know the fire of the font,
he burned with the heat of God;
by that heat he was joined to the waters,
dedicated to Christ by his deeds.
With the garment with which he covered the naked man
the King of heaven shone:
with a dirty rag is gained
that by which the sphere of stars shines.
How just an exchange!
The needy man repays with a star,
and the beggar prepares kingdoms.
Soon he attained the sacred things of life;
he made sport of the crowd of demons;
he commanded the dead to rise from their ashes:
corpses lived again at his touch.
Willingly he suffered scourges,
with which he wove himself a crown.
Forced to become bishop,
resisting, he took on the vow,
which holy faith fulfilled.
21. HYMN OF ST DIONYSIUS.
To Dionysius Christ gave
as many victories as wars.
The exile is a citizen of the godly,
a sharer in the city above.
Constantius the tyrant once
drove the bishop from his see.
He did not yield to the violent man;
his faith grew through dangers.
This is what holy confession grants:
punishment hands you over to good fortune,
you buy what you long for with misfortune.
Persist, torturer, you who help:
this light is granted through refusing to deny.
O how blessed is adversity,
if exiles triumph like this!
From a revered martyr
that confessor differed in nothing.
Those whom a lingering death afflicts
fly up to the reward of death.
Slow cooking loses nothing:
it secretly enters what is hidden.
Grief is a life-giving death;
passing away is a swift cure.
He laughed at the emperor's fury,
hurried from place to place, his faith unshaken;
steadfast, he is led across the world
where the sun blazes most fiercely,
denied the means to drink.
From you, dread Lord, we receive
as if it were ours what you reward.
Send the saint to ask
for what you yourself will bestow on us.
EPIGRAMS.
1. EPITAPH OF A GOOD MAN.
Good by birth, shining in uprightness, and the founder of his name —
does he lie like this, tell me, grief, in a narrow tomb?
The hope of a great house is covered by a modest grave;
lofty heights are hemmed in by a little turf.
What use is grace in boys, what do life's thresholds offer?
Death comes without waiting for due order.
What did it profit him that he showed old age in tender years?
He has joined many deaths to his own.
He has died, alas, a youth, who wiped away the sins of life,
for God gave him life in the season of faults.
Look, you who perhaps fear the years of early youth:
his age did not hold back the conquering boy.
Leaving an example to the earth, snatched up to the stars,
how well he shows the right road to those who confess!
He passed twice ten winters and as many harvests,
he whom hostile fate suddenly took from our eyes.
2. EPITAPH FOR ABUNDANTIUS, A MAN OF ILLUSTRIOUS RANK.
He never perishes in death who survives the pyre by his merits;
the grave cannot contain a lofty soul.
Blood, honor, talent, uprightness, constancy, wealth —
with their many endowments they destroy destruction.
Though it is common to all, the good man does not feel the losses of the tomb.
The Fates gather in the threads they gave the wretched;
the hanging threads that bear the common people wear thin;
strong threads fall to the lot of the noble.
His venerable ways renewed the hoary ages of old,
and in turn bore a pure heart as a temple.
3. ON THE EPIGRAMS MADE FOR THE BOOKCASES OF LORD FAUSTUS.
You have composed fitting poems for your various books:
let the written page gladly receive what it bestows.
I cannot think who would not praise such modesty, Faustus,
when you give back whatever your reading has given you.
A mind ignorant of what is right always loses what is entrusted to it;
these things come back to teach upright ways.
Yet if you graciously admit my words, I will confess:
he who is strong in great things rightly shuns trifles.
Let the poets whom you portray be praised in polished verse,
let a manly tongue thunder in rhetorical figures;
as Paul taught that Christ is both man and God,
let him rejoice in the eloquence by which he surpasses all.
Let Attic doctrines be enriched through Greek thought,
and let learned Greece marvel at our glory.
Let ethics be told in terse lines, natural philosophy in precise ones;
let history, displaying history, point it out;
let comedy be measured with the file, heroic deeds with applause:
clear sayings suit your work.
No one else can do this; but to speak of Faustus will always
be the height of praise, if I rightly say what is well known.
4. [ON A CARRIAGE THAT THE BISHOP HAD GIVEN.]
The highest of bishops gives you, noble carriage.
It opens the way for great things and makes the omens favorable.
5. EPITAPH OF RUSTICA.
Rustica, pale fate has not taken you from everlasting life,
nor has it brought you to ruin by death.
Purer, without flesh, you will walk through the citadels of heaven.
So death ennobles the life of a chaste woman,
since — a wonder — your widowed years stood so firm,
when love of your husband was rightly turned to your son.
6. EPITAPH OF MELISSA.
Whoever rises above the conquered body dies, yet survives:
only sins impose on man the law of death.
Nothing of you perishes, virgin: your pure mind has given back the flesh,
which never lived in the service of the world.
Let funerals, tombs and pyres, the wages of sin, cease:
this passage from life to life is pleasing.
7. [THE BRONZE SERPENT ON THE CROSS.]
Slayer of death, leader of life, plant of salvation!
Look: behold, the serpent drives away poisons,
and what had once been for the wretched the form of punishment and the image of death
is for me sure salvation.
8. VERSES MADE AND WRITTEN IN THE BASILICA OF ST SIXTUS, WHICH BISHOP LAURENTIUS BUILT.
A bishop strong in talent, uprightness and modesty
adorned the gift with his merits and the lights of his life,
and, joining them to the cost of the work, set up this temple.
Fame does not slip away and scatter into uncertain hiding places,
but the law of an ancient deed lives on, increased through the ages,
since Sixtus graciously receives Laurence's gifts.
So the service that once fell to the saints endures:
this one offered a temple, which that one comes and consecrates.
9. LIKEWISE IN THE BASILICA OF THE SAINTS, BECAUSE THE BUILDINGS THAT HAD STOOD THERE [?] BEFORE HAD BURNED, AND SO IT WAS BUILT.
The mean roofs of before gave way to blessed flames,
if splendor comes through loss, if from flames rise roofs
that will house God, if what was lost grows
through harmless fires, if losses bring adornment.
What will the restorer be like, enlarged by crackling ruin?
Laurence, waging your own wars, conquer the fires.
The squalid ground would have lain hidden in a withered nook
if the caverns of the old state had kept their appearance.
But after heaven sent favorable flames,
these ashes drew it out into the light to be revered.
Turn your holy eyes here, father, you who preach that all things
must be consigned to the burning, and instruct by deeds those who are to be taught,
lest a mind ignorant of what is right should falter at words.
10. VERSES WRITTEN IN A HOUSE AT MILAN.
Two things are granted to houses to give them character through the ages:
if they shine with marble facing, or by the merit of their master.
Let grassy stones imitating green pasture
entice the eye with a nobler deceit;
let the work deceive by art, yet let nature rule the figures,
while she shapes the inner stuff of the stones into images;
let the master craftsman suffuse the white with a rosy face,
and paint well-proportioned limbs with scattered markings.
Gold, lofty roof, ivory, panels, coffered ceilings, gems:
human goods are not granted to glitter more brightly.
In the value of marble facing, chance even plays without law.
To stand firm by your character, believe me, will take labor.
11. [IN THE BASILICA OF THE APOSTLES AT NOVARA.]
Behold, the (ancient) temple shines that was squalid before,
whose old face a new light has refashioned.
Who has lost an ancient shrine through religion,
when, the idols driven out, it rightly holds the Godhead?
You gods to whom this place lay open, leave the seats you held.
What Victor made, a victor holds everywhere.
His successor rightly added to its adornment by his deeds as well,
you, Honoratus, who bear a name drawn from your character.
He who carries a clouded heart full of viper's venom
is not allowed to build fair roofs for God.
12. [LIKEWISE IN A HOUSE AT MILAN.]
Learn from whose streams the narrow house has drunk,
so that with its modest porticoes it surpasses great halls.
Built by the zeal of the highest bishop, it gleams;
it possesses Laurence's own day.
Splendid roofs raised by wealth rise only to ruin;
what comes from the Lord knows no setting.
Hardly will decay, the companion of old age, ever wear this away,
the glory of its maker, because he founded it well.
Story, never silent about the great, preserves
what, outlasting bronze, may carry his name to the stars.
He was always a guardian of strict integrity,
fearsome to faults and gentle to suppliants;
vice never bent him, but pity always did;
with a steady face he gave judgment everywhere.
He rebuked crimes with a look and comforted the contrite;
he bore lips that knew your secret.
His mother poured him from her womb into the heavenly court;
withdrawing her own breasts, she gave him over to other breasts.
Hoary ages were amazed at the venerable bishop:
by character he already was what he now is by office.
Who has happily left dwellings long possessed?
What house has grown like this when bereft of its master?
Taking up the governance of the court, he was snatched away and obtained, unpurchased,
what is sought at the price of the mind.
Now the place keeps what it drank in with a watering draught,
guarding the good fortune once swallowed down.
Whoever at once succeeded as dweller and heir,
this house gave him a lucky footing as he entered.
Learn what such fellowship offers toward a holy life,
if dedicated roofs make men pure.
Grant, almighty Father, through long ages, we pray,
that sure hope may come to pious guests;
that the white threads may not be darkened by our deserts,
nor the palm prepared for me halt at the turning posts.
Let him rise who, cherished in his own mother's womb,
came to the taste of life through your gifts.
You flood my heart even with a faint savor;
you make my tongue a witness of the blood.
Lofty strawberry trees burst into leaf in dark luxuriance,
though no farmer has pruned them with sickles.
Eloquence has stood as a sure index of nature
for one who thirsts to seek the fountain of the perfect.
Freedom is always unlocked by honorable studies;
nobility left unwrought lies hidden in darkness.
The earth would have kept the metal captive in its veins
had not the finder brought out into the open what he calls forth.
The pale miner has surrendered the tawny gold:
so he who polishes a free-born talent makes it his own.
Thus far, crossing the Ionian Sea with few oars —
now turn my skiff toward harbor, Thalia.
17. OVER THE MAIN DOOR OF THE DINING ROOM IN A HOUSE.
The sailor hangs the sea's gifts on his doorposts,
displaying on his own doors what the river yielded.
The hunter sets his iron javelin by the gates;
the soldier's entrance is adorned with a helmet.
On doors one learns a man's craft, valor, name and origin.
We are believed to be God's by the sign on our forehead.
So reveal our pursuit, you letters, guide of what is right,
that the house may not be silent about its master's talent.
You who carry the Latin dew in a well-satisfied breast,
behold here the winding waters of Helicon.
18. ON A DISH SHOWING A YOUNG MAN IN A CUIRASS ON A HORSE, HOLDING A VICTORY IN HIS HAND.
Behold, a victorious right hand holds a winged goddess:
he comes, and for his return he needs no weapons for the road.
The steed that bears the warrior on its back looks menacing,
but its terror, rendered in art, makes the kindly stranger smile. Let the famous race in the Hyperborean fields learn
the genius of nature when it sees these likenesses.
19. ON A MARBLE LION THAT SPOUTS WATER IN A HOUSE.
Behold a lion made gentle, his fierceness laid aside:
from his mouth he pours out water in obedience of heart.
Water flows from his jaws; his tooth chews draughts of death;
the beast, losing his nature, quenches our thirst.
While savage throats pour out glassy springs,
cruel hearts are washed in saving waters.
20. IN THE BAPTISTERY AT UGELLO, WHERE THE MARTYRS WHOSE RELICS ARE LAID THERE ARE PAINTED.
Armenius the founder, worthy of heavenly honor,
brought forth here a font of life-giving water.
Let us carry our inmost being filled with saving waters:
the wave once given has ensured that he who drinks shall not thirst.
The painter has brought to life bodies snatched away by burial:
let death, seeing living corpses, go off into the tombs.
Yet this place also embraces the limbs
of those whom the wall holds in likeness and the kindly mind holds in faith.
21. ON SEVEN SMALL DISHES SHOWING WILD BEASTS OR DIANA.
Delia, stag, boar, tiger, lion, heifer, leopard
bring courses to your table, learned friend.
22. ON A PLATTER WITH SEVEN BOWLS.
It keeps close-set borders for different foods,
while it encloses many dishes in various compartments.
What a joined arrangement divides by fixed boundaries,
how well one belly holds in silver!
23. ON ONE WHO COMMITTED A THEFT TO RECONCILE A SON TO HIS MOTHER.
Who, I ask, has ever checked a crime by a misdeed?
I embrace holy frauds that sow good seed,
when they break off cruel quarrels with skillful gain.
He who restores a son to his mother's love through a fault
is surely sending seeds of peace into hatreds.
By an inverted order, the fight is a deceptive concord,
when a pretended face of war brings peace.
24. ON ONE WHO WAS SAID TO BE THE SON OF A HARLOT AND AN ASS-DRIVER.
Gods, avert the threats that a hideous birth announces —
one whom a she-wolf bore, conceived of a filthy ass.
The mate who was her food filled her womb with offspring,
and the wild beast, squandering the law, bore young to a beast of burden.
What will a discordant mongrel do, breaking nature?
Who could say where the son should look for something to follow,
whom his father made a fool, and his shameless mother a thief?
By falling short of them he might have reached a noble height.
But believe me, your parents know you as their own in vices:
tongue-tied, timid, boastful, fit for frauds,
of a vast gullet, swallowing whatever is anywhere,
who, once he has accustomed his jaws to human blood,
opens them wide and does not turn his snout to cheap bullocks.
25. ON SOMEONE'S CUP SHOWING PASIPHAE AND THE BULL. IMPROMPTU.
Pasiphae, not forsaking the snow-white bullock even in art,
with your arms flung around his neck you beg him for kisses,
and, more beautiful though a mere image, you put real girls to shame;
the white ox outshines the silver with the brightness of his color:
love lives on, bull and woman without a real body.
26. ON ONE WHO NEVER GAVE A FEAST EXCEPT AT THE BURIAL OF A SON.
He who serves lavish dishes to his guests amid weeping
should celebrate an annual feast with great tears.
27. ANOTHER.
While his house stands, believe me, he never feeds so many —
he who fills tombs with his sons and tables with his friends.
28. ANOTHER.
Poor guests, pray for many sorrows:
there will be as many dinners as there are funerals.
29. AGAIN ON THE CUP SHOWING PASIPHAE AND THE BULL.
The woman caresses, the ox feels it, the limbs are stirred.
Art supplied the forms: who gave them souls?
30. ANOTHER.
Even as an image, shameless Venus, he keeps an unbending mind —
the bull — so that he holds back his muzzle from the lips pressed near.
31. ANOTHER.
If you have souls, painter, into which you put your art,
let a softer spirit be shut inside the bull, I pray,
if a strong heart is not granted to the wretched girl.
32. ON THE FACT THAT THE CONSUL MESSALA WAS GIVEN THE SURNAME ENNODIUS.
I have joined my name to the consul's dignity in place of a pedigree:
giving light to the calendar of consuls, I am worth more than the consular robe.
Why, palm-embroidered robe, do you bloom so proudly with your purple?
Our purple has given you more than your dye.
33. ON AN ADVOCATE WHO SPOKE AGAINST HIM.
Shameless man, why do you jumble everything with broken words?
Your smothered tongue paints your character.
You accept, you demand, you presume, you refuse, you burn.
You are sullen and fawning at once, strong and slack.
Anger, fear, rage and patience all at one time:
you wear so many faces with an empty heart.
34. VERSES WRITTEN AT UGELLO, WHERE ANGELS OFFER TO CHRIST THE SON OF ARMENIUS, WHO DID PENANCE.
Jesus receives the offering on whom he has bestowed pardon.
After sins, souls are God's burnt offerings.
Go on, boy, rising above your tender years with a good conscience.
A white life has earned holy bearers.
35. ON ONE WHO DISPARAGED THE GAULS IN HIS PRESENCE, BEING A VENETIAN SLANDERER.
You mock the Gauls, you ill-dyed offspring of the Veneti.
You have no whiteness: your mind is like your race.
You despise the innocent, you home-bred slave of a stained land;
but the snow of uprightness belongs to the sons of the Rhone.
36. AN EPIGRAM WRITTEN AS A SIGNATURE.
What the law of nature has given you as offspring, friend,
let the font of life-giving water give to me.
37. IN A HOUSE, BEFORE THE ORATORY.
You buy gains with losses, joys with mourning,
if you have undoubting faith in Christ.
38. BEFORE THE OIL STORE.
This is how a limb is anointed with shining olive oil:
nothing is more fitting before holy doors.
39. BEFORE THE GRANARY.
The granaries may be small, but the heart is larger than they.
By not sparing my wealth, I have earned riches.
40. BEFORE THE STAIRS.
Let those come who open their mind, with the figure as witness,
the sign by which a vow is always revealed.
41. BEFORE THE STOREROOM.
No pinching of a grudging mind opens the larder:
what lies hidden flows out through wide spaces.
XLII. Over the kitchen.
No sprawling kitchens serve me lofty luncheons,
nor does my belly keep many craftsmen busy.
We serve few dishes, but they surpass number in refinement,
and the table's glory brings no harm to health.
XLIII. Over the cellar.
A sober cellar, which keeps wine in laden jars,
strengthens bodies that walk on their own steady feet.
Let others' cups pour flames of anger into many;
warlike hearts grow gentle with our wine.
XLIV. At the entrance to the garden.
Look back, you who wind your steps through the pleasant greenery,
so that you may learn to rank the brilliance of an eloquent man above cultivated gardens.
The bud that smiles is the one painted with the purple of the tongue:
he who brings forth flowers in song has spring in midwinter;
through the ice his words breathe out warm west winds.
His words are drunk, soaked in gleaming purple dye.
In all things the purple of speech reigns;
water snakes bow their necks at the command of his mouth.
Since chilled hearts grow young again with rosy blood,
letters display youthfulness in cold limbs.
The learned man turns nature's gifts to his service:
ages, appearances, measures, seasons, shapes.
XLV. Inside the garden, above the threshold.
Let him praise the advantages of gardens with lavish spaces
whose hunger is sated by many cultivated acres.
The generous endowment of small gardens is richer, and surpasses the vast ones:
true nobility is that which shines in modest things.
Grace came to this enclosure, putting the open fields behind her,
and showed what care can do in narrow spaces.
At the entrance a portico blooms with green shade,
on which the vine-bearing god himself has poured out his spirit;
adorning the woven leaves with great clusters,
he joins comfort to summer coolness.
For lilies, laurels and olives mingled with rose beds
have, through cultivation, made it have a daylight of its own;
the golden earth has added to its offspring the wreaths
that show the brow of a triumphant victor crowned.
Let the man rich in wealth demand the rewards of a greater wish:
this is enough for us, what gives pleasure without deceit.
XLVI. On the necklace of the illustrious lady Firmina, which is shut in a septicium [?], so fine is it.
Its spirit flits, most slippery, in the gold drawn thin;
the wearied metal barely touches her white limbs.
The value given it by the panting furnace has struck down its weight.
XLVII. Another.
The master dissolved threads of gold into mists;
skilled hands enclosed tawny breezes.
XLVIII. Another.
Here the wind has gathered the limbs of precious metal:
what they have fashioned, the eyes fear and cannot take in.
XLIX. Another.
It is nothing, yet I hold it: my right hand refutes my sight.
A breeze is clasped in the tightened grip of the fingers.
L. On one who sent figs as a gift together with a token.
Your token sends the fruit of the condemned tree.
This dread food first stripped man bare,
and after the fraud, serpent, you menace the naked with your lot.
Spare the gifts, I pray; keep misfortunes and losses away.
Why do you think the fruit will harm a guiltless man's well-being?
The tree that once bore death then drove death away,
when Life hung nailed on its triumph-bearing branches.
LI. On an adulterer and effeminate man.
All the ages are preserved in Memphian fabrics:
Laurence never before served Nero,
nor did he who conquered the mighty flames with his body fear them.
LII. Another.
A man in face, a woman in gesture, but in leg both at once,
settling nature's quarrels by making no distinction,
you are a hare, and you trample the neck of so great a lion.
LIII. Another.
Get rid of your lying beard, little wife of the public,
lest manly lips cut into your earnings.
LIV. Another.
Behold a monster created by a mingled law,
of common gender — though better called "of every gender."
LV. Another.
A constant deceit plays in an ambiguous sex:
it submits as a woman; when it commits vile acts, it is a man.
LVI. In the baptistery of Milan.
Let him shine purer than the light of refined metal
who arranges gifts worthy to be given to God.
Laurence's life first stood firm in heated furnaces,
so that he might ennoble this charming work.
Marbles, paintings, panels, a lofty coffered ceiling —
he who shines in uprightness gave these himself to the church.
So the founder adds his character to the value of the building,
