as if you were to bring Chinese silks dyed with purple,
as a visiting light adorns gems set in their bezels,
whenever snow-white stone blushes more beautifully through art.
LVII. On Jovinian, who, though he had a Gothic beard, came out dressed in a Roman cloak. Extempore.
I marvel that a barbarian face takes on Roman dress,
and at races set side by side in one ill-matched body.
LVIII. Another.
The cloudy night of his face darkens the Roman garment:
his face has overwhelmed his clothes with its gloomy covering.
LIX. Another.
You rob noble cloaks of their dignity, you badly groomed man,
mixing discordant offspring in a hostile alliance.
LX. In the basilica of Saint Calimerus, when it was restored.
The roofs, set free, have won the light that was once held captive;
the building's face smiles, bearing no clouds.
Here recently came a gift close to starry heaven,
brought about by the ministry of Laurence the bishop,
whose life and buildings now have one and the same shape,
as in the rays of the sun form and color are alike.
Well done, restorer of old things! Go on, founder of new ones,
bright in face and in mind.
Under your leadership the roofs forswear their ancient decay;
a new spirit is held out to what was about to fall.
LXI. On a certain old enemy, foolish and well fed.
You prepare lavish luncheons, but you bristle with the filth of your tongue.
If, an idle shepherd, you procure the dishes,
ambitious hunger, squandering an exhausted fortune,
leaps upon the horns, if the master keeps silent.
LXII. On the same, because he devoured the wealth of the poor.
You who have grown fat on the entrails of the wretched and the blood of the poor,
why are the deaths of so many your feasts?
Truffles, partridges, crane, thrush, turtle-dove, sea urchin —
a thousand bodies do not fill your belly.
Ill-starred for many, you are called fortunate for yourself alone,
since the wretch's own belly will be his heir.
LXIII. On the same.
Polyphemus lived on human limbs, and took his delight
in men swollen with dark blood.
You, as the scene comes round again, bring back a like madness,
you to whom troops of the weak supply your fodder.
LXIV. On one who fed people in order to draw his friends over to himself.
To plunge the divine pair into death, the serpent offered food,
and, dreadful one, took away life by a gift.
So whoever soothes my labors, truly labors of paradise,
suffers the snares of the banquet:
there the friend he carried in his heart departs from him;
the host becomes the lodging of a dear gullet.
LXV. On the cunning Defensor.
You are unknown to men's wishes, and in the cloud of your heart you withdraw
from their eyes; though present, you must be searched for in your face,
and you know how, by roundabout ways, to be seen by no one,
giving poisons from honey-flowing lips.
"This I want," you say, when you do not; swearing you do not want what you desire,
you shake savage hearts in various ways,
skilled to outdo the Hydra in heads and Prometheus in shapes,
so that legend need no longer go back to the ancients:
you stir up wars, you grow fat on plunder seized, Defensor;
proud booty runs to your name.
LXVI. Preface to the whole poetic work which he composed.
While my anxious mind endures manifold surges
and I am made the slave of the glassy sea,
and while the stormy southwest wind, ferryman of the ebbing wave,
whirls me about like captured spoils,
a Pierian warmth fell upon my mind; soon Apollo's laurel
encircled my temples, which had lacked a garland;
then the clusters of green ivy reddened on my brow,
and I drank the soft murmurs of Castalian honey.
At once, laying aside the wasting cares in my breast,
I embrace praise, songs, and joy.
LXVII. On the fact that he wrote at the time of the vintage.
While my faithful servants store our new wine in jars
and sport at the press with fearless heels,
while they dye their soles in the blood of rosy Bacchus,
and the grape that wears tender tunics is split open,
not enduring idleness, I furrowed songs on Nile papyrus,
so that, when I die, the tomb may not hold me.
Having owned up to the drunken words of a tottering Thalia,
I am free of blame if she staggers in her feet.
The law of art, syllable and rhythm, suits the fasting;
none of the Muses keeps company with Bromius.
LXVIII. On a certain glutton who, unskilled himself, carped at his work.
I do not know why you do not spare holy labor, you fool,
keeping to your habit by leaping on it with your teeth.
You go on chewing me, but your belly gets no benefit from it,
for you are grasping at breezes in empty images.
The whirlpool of food receives nothing into cheeks bursting with grumbling,
or else overflows with vain motions.
Picking at the Phasian bird, at fish or sow's udders,
feed your moist gullet on steaming foods;
it pleases me, fasting, to compose my verses without belching:
let dishes of royal luxury sate you.
LXIX. On a eunuch tribune named Peregrinus, who wanders about everywhere.
Race, wealth and way of life are vouched for by witnesses, Tribune,
whenever we leave our old abode.
You, whom wandering has sent on across the nations you have traversed,
whom no house, however spacious, holds for a full day,
want to be called rich, lofty, handsome, a friend,
sent by the tides of an unknown Ocean.
Empty words fly about; no one comes to back you;
no proof discloses your sex or your homeland.
Beggar, old, timid, confused, wheezing:
use these names, since you have lost the true one.
LXX. Another on the same.
You can safely tell lies without a witness, Tribune:
the wind holds the tongue of one who lacks weight.
LXXI. Another on him, because he never stays put.
Nature's losses make the Tribune unstable:
he flies off from here again unless chains hold him.
Take on a little ballast, poor wretch, when the west wind comes:
no root is of any use to help you.
LXXII. Another on him.
The eunuch begs a shameful living through the crossroads:
he has nothing from which to bring seed to the earth.
The countryside keeps great seeds in its plowed-up limbs,
and the harvest returns multiplied in its yield.
In vain does the cut man break the backs of the fields with the plowshare,
unless, as he splits them, he scatters wheaten offspring.
LXXIII. On the fact that, though he himself had Gallic parents, he loved to eat geese.
Here is a battle of birds, where the goose is slain by a Gaul — a cock:
the bird pays the penalty for an old betrayal.
In its slaughter you exact the price of its voice of long ago, wicked man:
the one that gave the Romans life is dying.
LXXIV. On the inconstancy of the clergy.
He who knows the faces of the sea and the number of the sand,
whom no woman can deceive by swearing,
to whom the throng of stars that watches lovers' paths is known,
and Cynthia by her sure horns —
even he cannot keep track of the faces, names and characters
which the clergy change within a short time.
LXXV. On a wicked man who loved horses.
He delights in horses, this dissuader from right, squanderer of fairness,
who with overweening zeal takes worthy names away
to give them to nags, setting a rump against holy names.
But what this man of wicked mind reckons as beasts is far from it:
the character of a breed persists, as pedigrees produce it.
LXXVI. On the cunning man who was called Defensor.
So that a hospitable deceit with hidden tricks may catch asps,
the image of death lurks under a show of play.
A cunning shadow lures out the provoked pests,
and war is waged with charming beginnings.
Believe me, that is just how Defensor conducts his battles:
he accuses with a smile, he kills calmly.
LXXVII. On the deeds and life of the lord bishop Ambrose.
Ambrose the bishop practiced what he taught, surviving in merit and honor,
in character and in genius;
his dewy tongue shone with royal purple,
painting with its own spring the buds it chose.
Crowned, he wore bright garlands on his brow,
and with his mouth he prepared a work studded with gems.
He instructed the peoples by his bearing, his uprightness, his modesty;
he cherished, he took heed, he struck, he admonished.
As the gravest dangers call for the service of the voice,
so slight faults are pursued by one who keeps silent.
Girded with swords, safe under the weight of a shield,
he enclosed his breast in woven steel.
His sword, cutter and foe of vices, has strength;
the viper does not touch that man's scaly back.
LXXVIII. On Saint Simplician the bishop, his successor.
Ambrose, leaving behind the duties of a widowed people,
handed them over to your care, Simplician.
By the successor's help the vitals of the despoiled realm
grew through the merit of another age,
and as long quiet, with sparing west winds, strengthens an aged ash
so that it does not fear war,
so this fortunate recruit, called to his first training when already white-haired,
did not degenerate or bend the ancient crown.
With a fervent soul in chilled marrow he feared nothing.
The bishop's virtue has an old age in flower;
he trod the plains of earth under an open roof,
while by his character and devotion he touched the stars.
LXXIX. On blessed Venerius, who followed.
Venerius came as a youth, a model of chastity to be followed,
in no way a slave to his name.
His strong limbs grew faint under an aged judge;
age had destroyed the boy who was still there.
After he mounted the lofty supports of the bishop's chair,
young as he was, he expounded hoary doctrines to the peoples.
Golden figures of a rich tongue flowed from him;
the sun of his life made his eloquence shine.
When the womb of the church had swelled with the seed of the Word,
the nourishment of apostolic milk was not lacking.
LXXX. On the succession of the venerable Marolus.
Marolus, who drank the waters of the distant Tigris,
who had seen the radiance in the moist lodgings of the font,
whom toil had strengthened under Syria's own sky,
begins as bishop with countless endowments:
watchful, intent, fasting, provident, ardent;
that he kept to his old way of life was enough for his office.
Whenever the tender mouth tastes what is honorable,
what was a matter of command passes into affection.
The land once mighty, founded by blessed fathers,
illuminates the world with noble offspring.
LXXXI. On Martinian, bishop and worshipper of God.
Mind of snowy milk, manifest likeness of a dove,
a serpent in shrewdness — Martinian, farewell.
When the slippery breezes of the wavering crowd called for you,
they found you afraid lest you be deemed worthy of election.
He alone spoke against it, with the world as judge,
a man who, in order to gain the kingdom, did not earn the victory.
Promptly led to the threshold of great honor,
the exile is enrolled among the citizens of heaven.
Afterwards, purer still, he built two churches for the saints,
which he commanded to have daylight though the light was shut in.
LXXXII. On the venerable bishop Glycerius.
Suffused with vermilion and blushing through his excellent deeds,
Glycerius follows with a maiden's face.
While he stains his pure appearance with a blood-red dew,
his face, painted on the cheeks, pleased by its simplicity.
Wearing a gleaming brow sprinkled with saffron,
he had tinged his joyful features with modest marks.
Having obtained the scepter that the witnessing image had granted him,
he whom the purple of his mind had revealed as fit to rule
departed hence: the people were happy for scarcely a short time,
but he was sent once more to the service of the Great One.
LXXXIII. On Saint Lazarus the bishop.
So that Lazarus might tread under foot the summits of the dread world,
summoned by the people's voices, he came forth, stern, into their midst;
his brow, little given to joy, had marked him out as an enemy of vices,
punishing faults with silent eyes.
Looking upon those who had fallen, he wiped away the clouds of their life;
often he gave care in the service of the wound.
He who committed a crime in hidden caves did not lie hidden;
even when absent, he was everywhere a torturer to crimes.
To the innocent he bloomed, serene, with a gentle light,
like a mirror casting their own face back on the guilty.
LXXXIV. On Eusebius the bishop, friend of God.
Eusebius, a stranger, succeeded to the territory of the Ligurians,
drawn by the friendship of a people unknown to him.
He was a Greek, of those whom the Titan beholds at his neighboring rising,
as he shakes the waters from his flaming head.
Mild, composed, generous, devout, upright, bold,
he believed that not to give was a perpetual loss.
He wept in pity over poverty, he smiled on one who had plenty,
sharing joy and sadness with all.
Fame, the herald of his work, announces this man to a world ready to speak of him,
drawing nations from their stations.
LXXXV. On Gerontius, a simple man, bishop.
After the seat of the church was won by you, Gerontius,
your predecessor did not fear death as he died.
Through your renewal he returns; pale fate suffers death;
he lives after his death by the worth of his disciple.
Joined to the husbandmen, you cultivated the seeds of life,
and the creeping darnel did not take away the rich pastures.
He who has put into the common stock the sustenance the best of laws commands
buys heaven with earthly fruits.
You crushed the error of the mind by the law of labors;
not enduring idleness, you are borne aloft by your virtues.
LXXXVI. On the venerable bishop Benignus.
Show forth the sure name that the mind has bestowed, Benignus;
whoever calls you by it will be a witness to your merit.
When hoary faith tells of the man, it discloses his deeds;
one in awe of his child says nothing by chance.
Foreseeing the future, parents' wishes do not err;
they turn the endearments of their offspring into truth.
Earlier he sat as a senator among the fathers, to the senate's applause;
he lifted up his head, set above the saints.
But by a cruel thumb he was cut down, like a flower by the plow:
hope, glory and genius fell from the doorway.
LXXXVII. On the most blessed man, bishop Senator.
He who surpassed robes of state, the throne and the Gabine girding,
outstanding beyond consuls — behold, Senator is here:
swift genius, care for rounded speech,
the prize of virtues, a model of chastity,
who brought into the light the hidden things of books
and the closed mysteries of the prophet, in whatever form he chose.
Sent to the secret places of the farthest world, with reverent zeal
he healed what had been torn apart.
Then the East, confessing itself conquered by a foreign light,
stood fixed at the sight of another lamp.
LXXXVIII. On the lord Theodore, bishop, a man of every virtue.
You, the sure light of your people, you, the most faithful hope in all affairs,
you, Theodore, the vigor of an apostolic bishop,
a heap of virtues, a shining substance of truth,
whom toil displays in amassed learning:
foreseeing, ready, strong, tranquil, friendly,
composed, simple — you, good and wise,
prophetic: your heart always knew the future;
evil, once detected, flowed away when you laid it bare.
You, whom the fierce who tread the summits of the world feared,
loved, scorning the harshness of a haughty brow.
LXXXIX. [On Laurence, the bishop still living.]
There remains one whom the glorious King may preserve for a long age.
XC. [To Deuterius.]
Guardian of command, giving life to the strings with your singing thumb
through the measures — for you, teacher, I have compelled the speaking threads
to serve a song under the strokes of the plectrum.
Cirrha, mighty through Phoebus, the devout throng of the clear spring —
that you will always be to me, you who bring closed hearts into
remote services and fill them with a favoring power.
I pray, receive kindly the voice you demanded,
and with you as judge grant a reward to words wrung out of me.
XCI. On marbles in patchwork.
With the stones' entrails forced together by a law of mixture,
the craftsmen's efforts create nature.
The marbles have stiffened into a solid out of broken limbs;
their spirit is gathered from parts into a single veneer.
He who could compose one appearance from varied fragments
has brought stone into obedience.
XCII. On a platter bearing his own image.
The likeness of Ennodius gives value to rich metals.
XCIII. On his basin.
The water gives birth to thirst, the water the gleaming basin serves.
XC, line 1: cf. Tibullus II [?] 5.3, and Zingerle, Ovid, vol. I, p. 106.
XCIV. On the horse he received, a Hunnish one.
Warlike steed, reared under the frozen pole,
carrying your breast dry through the middle of the Don,
chewing hoary grasses in frosty haunts,
you whom valor, by the law of the sky, trained for itself:
after nations subdued, after such great rivers of blood,
you have a new master, but the toil itself remains.
Leave the war-trumpet, I pray, you who are now to bear blessed songs:
a captive, you are sent to the services of peace.
You have nothing to do with wars: bugles commend death:
what good is it always to love the slaughter you have known?
XCV. Epitaph of Saint Victor, bishop of Novara.
Victor by the name given you, by your merits, by your contest,
you look down on the lands weighed down by stained seed.
Possessor of a body yet free of the flesh's vices,
you tamed the slippery world by subduing your limbs,
tranquil, patient, a corrector, provident, keen.
Here, returning your ashes to the tomb, summoned on high,
your spirit rejoices, shining in the citadel of heaven.
From the brow of Olympus it looks with pity on the grave,
whence, looking back on the funeral of a world you triumphed over,
you will grant rewards to limbs released from their snares.
XCVI. On a certain Roman who wanted to be a teacher.
No study came to you as a sign of natural talent;
no letters refine the dealings of your brutish tongue:
never a pupil — tell me, if you can, how are you a teacher?
XCVII. On a certain old woman.
When cold blood dies in a living body,
when the ice of years dries up the nourishment of the womb,
and the useful blood that guards the seed has fled the loins,
why, withered Galla, are you joined to a young husband?
The hope of a child will perish in the bedchamber for your mate.
For, pretending that a false offspring lives within your slack wrinkles,
you, pregnant, deliver a child as a banquet for the sewer.
This is what your belly has produced, for your husband to put to his lips.
XCVIII. On the ring of the illustrious lady Firmina.
Nothing deceives by pretending: what the right hand fashioned is real.
By art the hare flees the motionless hound standing there;
a golden fury, set among raging bears, laughs;
the lion, to be worn on hands, rages, its wrath gentler.
The spirit of the work recognizes its mistress, the metal serving her.
She tames wild beasts while she feeds the needy people.
XCIX. [On Albinus.]
You see that Albinus gave inscriptions after the tombs,
he who slays death with living merits.
Illustrious man, while you, O prince, subject the powers of the magister to him,
that place has truly become a place of burial.
C. [On a hunting dog and a lamb.]
Here a certain clever little fellow is called Creticus,
keen of nose, swift of step, fearsome of jaw,
fearless, marking the tracks with his snout pressed down:
wherever stag, roe-deer, hares, wolf or she-bear roam,
he finds them, and the wary beast is caught in its warm lair.
After such great battles he is mocked by the flight of a little lamb:
a soft creature of the flock outran the swift hound by a trick.
CI. On little dishes.
While he paints so well so many of Jupiter's seductions, so many crimes alive in figures,
the craftsman's right hand is itself depraved.
The silver's value lies in preserving ancient wickedness,
lest anything pure prevail over what Jupiter did by stealth.
Nothing is forgiven by time; the monuments of crimes rise again;
he who fashions the faults of old gives lessons by examples.
CII. [Another.]
If the divine adulterer then took on so many faces,
he first deceived himself with false images:
what would a god not have violated with a counterfeit body,
whose very form delights in its own adultery?
CIII. [On Pasiphae and the Minotaur.]
Venus is not wronged: nature's bonds stand firm;
the counterfeit heifer of Daedalus' craft lies idle.
Living by ingenuity, the two-formed cow does not moo,
and the counterfeit wood gives the heifer no real coupling.
See, once again a woman, a wife, submits to a bull:
the hearts of beasts sigh with human flames.
Once again the vast neck takes the bronze yoke upon it:
how it sweated, exhausted, with the strap drawn tight!
CIV. [On Deuterius the grammarian.]
Figure, head, face — Deuterius the master is all of these;
that teacher is famed for countless gifts.
Let his genius, perfect in every respect, excuse his tongue:
that he cannot speak only displeases the wicked.
They boast that the master does not know the art of grammar:
being simple, he teaches better by his character.
The orator's work and the stony heights of Tully
he has not touched: the lofty man loves no rhetors [?].
For his pupils his face is enough, and his revered, silent
baldness: they behold the full light of Phoebe.
CV. On the birthday of the child Arator. Extempore.
Rightly do you cultivate your own birthday, handsome Arator:
if you did not cultivate, would you be a ploughman?
CVI. On a certain man of uncertain calling and shameful life.
Deceitful in so many things, why do you chatter, two-formed magpie,
half-man, who weave shameful deeds with trembling loins?
What is your calling? What sex have you ever kept to?
What do you not falsely claim to be, man and woman, holy and profane?
CVII. Verses sent to Agnellus, a man of sublime rank. Extempore.
Whoever has stained bright affection
with a sullying dye, may he for that bear a tongue
scorched by the torches of Christ the judge,
his mouth entombed.
He tears apart every pact as he presses on, ever lively in deceit,
bearing with ill grace whatever a calmer order demands.
Leave behind, I pray, my friend, manners worthy of the lowest rabble;
follow the path of your blood and keep what you have pledged.
Ennodius to Agnellus.

Until your diligence gave its command, these uncollected pieces kept their health by staying to themselves. Having resolved in advance that they should be given to no one, either to read or to copy, I held up my hands against all who asked for them; now, won over by love for you, I have sent them. You will keep my modesty at its post if you read them over, but you will bring it to utter ruin if you copy them.
Love has loosed the bonds that another once tied:
an ancient law gives way only to a law that follows it.
109. [On His Own Verses.]
Never through long ages, by fruit-bearing dithyrambs,
have the blessings of Castalia flowed into me.
As I compose sad songs with hungry lips,
why, new hope of the Aonian stream, do you goad me on?
But if you rejoice that the thread of the Fates has changed,
show me now, Muse of Pegasus, a horn-hoofed steed
to carry its winged body over the dewy grass
without bending the tender crops beneath its tread:
tall, strong, handsome, well suited in its paces.
If that comes my way, Muse, you will soon please me.
You are sent to a generous rich man to ask a small thing:
unless you come back rejoicing, Muse, bid me farewell.
110. On the Castle of Bishop Honoratus.
A bishop's stronghold is life's surest hope.
What harm can assail one whose guardian is holy?
Here the shield is a buckler: far from here, Bellona, withdraw!
What stands firm by merits no battles can weigh down.
Here the Founder strengthens the walls, the Maker the defenses.
Let whoever hastens here in fear fear nothing.
111. On the King's Garden.
Right hand mighty in war, full of famous triumphs,
by which all that fled from obedience has fallen,
you who make lofty fame secure with scattered blood,
you whom both mildness and the bearing of arms have brought praise:
after reddening the vast arena of the battlefield,
you now till the fields, painting them with purple bloom.
You deal out fruits to the shrubs in your own purple,
you give fruit to the plants through your nobility.
See, the humbler turf boasts of a rich branch,
while the bite in the wood nurtures noble seeds.
Cut away with iron, another shoot blossoms for you:
a dowry gleams on the once bare trees now wedded.
The plants know their gardener in advance; mute things speak:
what the prince has touched has spring in the midst of ice.
The mighty earth exults and shows for whom the tree has grown:
here the master is revealed by its offspring and his genius.
Sleepless serpent who guard the acres of the Hesperides,
you offer golden gifts to fasting banquets.
Who would pluck the offspring of the grove with poison for its guard?
A grove made safe by death, believe me, no one approaches.
Here, Piety, you make common what you alone have provided.
Where bellies are full, hunger does not know how to come.
112. On a Certain Blind and Dissolute Man.
With your eye-socket dug out, displaying the running wound where your sight was,
you go about, pestilent one, wearing a buried face.
Your blind face is led around among countless friends:
those who look at you rightly grieve with their eyes.
Drunk, you enrich your chin with a sodden stream;
you carry about lips filthy with thick dung.
Seek no kisses; keep back your damp stench:
because of you I could wish to lose what I can see.
Who would think foul flames could gather in his eyes?
He sees nothing, yet keeps straight on the road of crimes.
113. On His Old Horse.
Our steed, made steadier by the guidance of years,
now carries a young man with gentle obedience.
Grown old, he lowers a soft back for his rider:
age has made him steady in his gait.
114. On the Whip of the Boy Arator.
A learned mind has fastened to a whip the things that win the world,
adorning its blows with ennobling wealth.
115. Another.
Whoever is beaten with metals of silver and gold
mingles greedy joys with his weeping.
116. Another.
Tawny gold is enclosed within teeth of silver:
let no one scorn to suffer such beautiful blows.
117. Epitaph of the Lady Mellisa, an Illustrious Woman.
In birth, mind, wealth, beauty, virtue and modesty,
I alone was such a woman as all would wish for.
Of the world I bore in my body only what is lawful,
adorning my chastity with chaste offspring.
Victorious by gentleness, I held a strong husband,
turning your rights, Severus, to my [?].
The children I bore I left joined to lofty lineage.
As holy women pray, I die before my husband.
I have lost nothing; I remain alive after the pyre:
death never comes upon the blessed to harm them.
And my name is sweet: from my deeds I am called Mellisa.
This name, given by right, flowed from my own character.
118. On a Certain Fool Who Was Called Virgil.
So far has the fame of ancient Maro declined
that our age has put you forward as Virgil.
119. Another.
If so holy a name is given to a foolish manikin,
the glory of our forebears will turn into disgrace.
120. Another.
The fool rejoices in the poet's captured pedigree.
He is not Virgil, yet that is what he is called.
121. Another.
Whenever you are called by another man's name, madman,
if you have any sense, take care not to answer.
122. Another.
Why do you falsely call yourself our Virgil, you wretch?
You cannot be Maro, but you can be a moron.
123. For a Chamber, Above Books Set in Order.
This is the path that prepares power on high,
light of modesty, food of the mind, a torch, a remedy, a splendor.
Those painted with the dregs of the world do not know how to keep to it.
Whoever binds his neck with this strap stands free.
This hoe adorns the vein of shining blood.
124. Against Claudianus, on Mules.
Look here at the swift daughter of the rushing Rhône
bowing her neck to the reins of your words.
At a word of command she flies, at a word of command she halts,
for her will is held captive by her ears.
She would feel chains, were she not held by the bit of the voice
and so through hearing lost the wantonness of her breed.
When a shout serves for the spur and a shout for the reins,
her free limbs yield obedience to the tongue.
There is no need of straps: the sure bond of speech
ties the hard mouth of the fettered beast.
125. On the Ass and the Mare.
She is forced to bring forth from her own womb an alien offspring
and to suckle the young of a foreign breed:
a quarrel of natures that lie far apart.
126. Another.
The mother, scarcely aware, bore an unknown offspring,
a cheating of nature by a nobler trick.
127a. Another.
The compact of birth has joined two different kinds:
stocks of different natures forced together under a mingled law.
127b. Another.
This mule is a twofold beast, but single in body.
128. On His Ride by Night in Summer.
The people of the stars had not yet lost their light
to the light of the sun, but in the lap of the deepening night
were spreading their ruddy hair, soaked with dew;
milk-white Cynthia was shining in her saffron chariot,
undoing whatever her brother's course had traced;
a silent splendor was blooming as the gift of night,
breaking with its coolness the scorching season of Cancer:
when, longing to cast off the burden of my cares,
I was called by the painted face of the lovely countryside.
I mounted a horn-hoofed steed that even Cyllarus could scarcely match,
who outstrips the breezes of heaven with his smooth running,
whose rider runs through the byways without being shaken,
flying while sitting still, as the feet press steadily on.
129. On the Litter of Viola, Wife of Bassus.
How constant the beauty this wandering shelter keeps!
Whatever value it has is lent it by its mistress.
For the tawny metal glows with the light of Viola:
its owner scatters her rays everywhere.
130. Epitaph of Euphemia.
She overwhelms the tomb; she lives on after death through her deeds,
she who put nothing mortal into her conduct.
Euphemia, the earth embraces your limbs,
but how well your mind is joined to the snow-white choirs!
Destruction itself has perished: the harshest lot is made a slave
when a life that knew no evil overcomes fate.
She was fruitful in marriage; widowed, by examples
of chastity she made her daughter love God.
131. On a Sword in a Staff.
We carry a staff with a sword craftily hidden inside:
how well death lies concealed beneath a tunic of wood!
You carry protection, because you are held a terror to all:
what refuses service to others is peaceable toward us.
132. On Boethius Girt with a Sword.
In your hands the substance of rigid iron grows limp,
and steel melts away like flowing water.
The unwarlike right hand of Boethius softens swords:
it was a sword just now, believe me; now it is a distaff.
The javelin you carry, shameless one, turns into a thyrsus.
Steadfast for Venus, give up the help of Mars.
133. On an Ivory Ostomachion.
Men's hearts, vexed by this light torment, wilt away:
it is proper for girls to play at it.
They break apart what the elephant sent from the Marmaric fields;
the work, scattered into fragments, is soon made whole again.
The tender ones learn to make sport of punishment with guile:
for to laugh at the gift of death is a woman's way.
They know how to shut a thousand things in a narrow box;
all this ivory here, woman, is the chest of your heart.
134. On a Bird Sitting on the Foam of the Po and Passing Along.
Rising against the curb of its banks, the bonds of nature,
the river had by chance overflowed in a swollen flood.
Forcing its flowing waters to harden into foam,
it bore scaly backs upon its powerful waters.
When a bird, trusting, settled on that soft round surface,
giving its wings a rest, it pressed the waters in safety.
The sea supplies from its own substance a boat to the one who treads it,
as a wet little skiff carries a dry bird.
135. On the Tomb of the Emperor Majorian.
Since fortune presses ever more heavily, in her wrath
she has granted a tomb, Majorian, to your remains.
Look to the huge masses of the pyramids for the unworthy;
leave humble tombs to pious princes.
136. On a Horse from the Po.
All you horn-hoofed steeds whom warlike lands produce,
and whose blood-stained flanks the waves wash clean,
you who have tamed the icy back of the deep Tanais,
whose hooves tread its mighty waters:
behold, here is a steed of the Po, to whom, if the judge be fair,
the Haemonian horses nurtured by the northern air must yield.
The horse that crops the grass in frosty haunts
comes off unequal on both counts, in merit and in beauty.
He steps gently, handsome in his comely limbs,
and delights the eye, sweet in his obedience.
Let legend no longer praise the Phasian breed,
nor let foreign names hold their heads high.
137. On a Drunken Princeps of the Praetorian Prefecture Who Carried a Vine-Staff.
True honor granted him the vine, but the wood
does not give the vine's gifts to a fasting service.
138. Another.
As a prince carries his scepter, so his right hand carries the vine:
let a divine crown of wineskins adorn his head.
139. Another.
Here, a dry vine-bearer, I clasp my master's mother,
who, though her breasts are squeezed, denies me wine.
140. Another.
Alas, how often has the fruitless vine mocked
my hot lips, refreshing me with nothing but its name!
141. Ennodius to Honoratus the Princeps.
Drinker, you hide your vice behind the faults of the land:
you cannot get drunk while spewing up Ligurian wines.
While sodden Bacchus fills your burning breast,
our cups only proclaim a mighty thirst.

142. On the Letter of the Lord Ambrose against Symmachus concerning the Altar of Victory, when Symmachus, Seeking Her Worship, Was Defeated. Composed on the Spur of the Moment and Sent to the Lord Faustus, Praetorian Prefect.
Victory takes the palm of eloquence from her friend.
She passes to Ambrose: the goddess's anger favors more.
143. Verses of the Lord Faustus.
Whoever calls a man a drinker in the land of the Ligurians is mistaken:
does a man who drinks Ligurian wines really drink wine?
144. Verses of Messala.
Accept our little verses, Ennodius, my closest friend,
so that you do not fail to return the book to us:
do not stain your refinement, Maximus, by refusing to return
what you too promised us long ago.
145. Of the Lord Ennodius.
If you were willing, Messala, to open yourself to me in your studies,
there would be no lack of books, my sweet friend, to give you.
A grossly unjust mind takes from one who loves it what it would only despise,
and no gift is welcome that one's talent shuns.
146. Of the Lord Ennodius.
He who asks for a grammar book about broken verse
is eager to have sound feet.
Oh, that by our gift the Muses might one day
have sure joys from you, my boy!
Unless I am mistaken, even those whom learning visits only in their dreams
avoid composing a club-footed verse.
147. On Honoratus.
I, the wife of Flasco, dowered with casks of Falernian,
my breast ever filled with unending Lyaeus,
who worshipped Bacchus devoutly with drenched lips,
soothing the swollen deity with belched-up new wine,
am shut, well aware of it, beneath the covering of a dry tomb:
yet among those above I have a noble husband, euhoe,
whom blessed cups could never pass by.
If the fates preserve this man, we both live on for you.
148. Epitaph of the Lady Dalmatia.
Death itself dies whenever a virgin is carried to the tomb.
The only road to death is servitude to sin.
By Dalmatia's merits rebellious nature was conquered;
with a nobility surpassing her birth she possesses heaven.
It is enough to have trampled the world while in a body of the world,
and to have yielded nothing to vices of what was taken from vice.
She outshone the light of her lineage with the sun of chastity;
her mind was united with her holy resolve.
149. On the Font of the Baptistery of Saint Stephen and the Water That Comes through the Columns.
See, without a cloud it rains beneath the roof in a calm shower,
and a clear sky supplies the waters.
Streams flow down over the sacred marble,
and see, the stone gives birth to dew again.
For a dry pergola pours forth flowing springs,
and once more water from above comes to those reborn.
Holy water streams down through heavenly recesses,
brought here by the ministry of Bishop Eustorgius.

150. [Ennodius's Apology for His Praises.] Let anyone who is surprised that I have overstepped the bounds of duty in praising my friends remember how imperious affection always is, and that the force of love does not obey the laws of intention. And surely, if he asks the reason for what I have done, he will call devotion what was masquerading as excess.
So that eagles may bring forth fully formed young,
the life-giving warmth within breaks the tender egg.
Then the devoted, tireless father tears open the cramped dwelling,
so that by his care he may bring forth again those he produced from the womb.
Soon the same judge summons Phoebus as witness of their lineage,
and, searching them with the light, finds an inner light.
In just the same way a parent's care sets boys
sprung from lofty lineage before the rays of learning.
See how well and how steadily the tender ones
take up the battle with the flames, outdoing the lightning with their gaze.
151. [On Two Houses Joined Together.]
One house, divided into a double building, is joined together,
and parts the work that it so well unites.
In twin dwellings a single holy glory shines,
and honor is united out of things divided.
So that sacred uses should be neither far apart nor confused in one place,
a generous lot gave a fixed site a double number.
